P-Act-Beta.why: A plain rule. A $\beta$ step changes only thread $i$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

P-Act-New.title: P-Act-New
P-Act-New.meaning: If $M(i) \xrightarrow{\mathsf{new}\,c} e'$ and $c \notin C \cup \mathsf{echans}(M)$, then $(C, M) \to (C \cup \{c\}, M[i \mapsto e'])$.
P-Act-New.why: Both ends of $c$ start in thread $i$, so $c$ is internal to the process and joins $C$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

sem.fresh-global.title: Global freshness
sem.fresh-global.meaning: $c \notin C \cup \mathsf{echans}(M)$, so $c$ is neither restricted nor mentioned by any thread.
sem.fresh-global.why: Channel names are global. If $c \in \mathsf{fchans}(M(j))$ for some $j$, the new channel would share its name with a channel thread $j$ uses.
sem.fresh-global.breaks: Reusing a name some thread still mentions merges two channels into one, and an action on one channel synchronizes with an action on the other.

args.name: c
args.meaning: The name of the channel being created.

args.name: C
args.meaning: The restricted channels of the configuration.

args.name: M
args.meaning: The thread map of the configuration.

P-Act-Spawn.title: P-Act-Spawn
P-Act-Spawn.meaning: If $M(i) \xrightarrow{\mathsf{spawn}\,v} e'$ and $j \notin \mathrm{dom}\,M$, then $M$ becomes $M[i \mapsto e'][j \mapsto v\,\ast]$.
P-Act-Spawn.why: The event is $\mathsf{solo}_i\,(\mathsf{spawn}\,v)\,j$, so only thread $i$ takes part.
P-Act-Spawn.example: $\mathsf{spawn}\,(\lambda u.\,e)$ adds a thread $j$ running $(\lambda u.\,e)\,\ast$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

args.name: j
args.meaning: The identifier of the new thread, $j \notin \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

P-Act-Msg.title: P-Act-Msg
P-Act-Msg.meaning: $M(i) \xrightarrow{o!v} e'$, $M(j) \xrightarrow{\overline{o}?v} f'$, $i \neq j$ give $M[i \mapsto e'][j \mapsto f']$, with no condition on $C$.
P-Act-Msg.why: In a typed process both ends of $c$ are held inside only when $c \in C$, so dropping the condition $\mathsf{ech}\,o \in C$ adds no step to typed processes.
P-Act-Msg.example: The client sends on $a$ and the server receives on $a'$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: j
args.meaning: The identifier of the partner thread, $j \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$ with $j \neq i$.

args.name: o
args.meaning: The end of the sender, the receiver acts on $\overline{o}$.

args.name: v
args.meaning: The payload, the same value in both labels.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

args.name: f'
args.meaning: The term of thread $j$ after its step.

P-Act-Close.title: P-Act-Close
P-Act-Close.meaning: If $M(i) \xrightarrow{o\,\mathsf{end}} e'$, $M(j) \xrightarrow{\overline{o}\,\mathsf{end}} f'$ and $\mathsf{ech}\,o \in C$, then $C$ becomes $C \setminus \{\mathsf{ech}\,o\}$.
P-Act-Close.why: After both closes no thread holds an end of $\mathsf{ech}\,o$, so the channel leaves $C$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: j
args.meaning: The identifier of the partner thread, $j \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$ with $j \neq i$.

args.name: o
args.meaning: The end closed by $i$, with $\mathsf{ech}\,o \in C$.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

args.name: f'
args.meaning: The term of thread $j$ after its step.

P-Act-Choice.title: P-Act-Choice
P-Act-Choice.meaning: If $M(i) \xrightarrow{o \lhd b} e'$ and $M(j) \xrightarrow{\overline{o} \rhd b} f'$ with the same $b$, then $M$ becomes $M[i \mapsto e'][j \mapsto f']$.
P-Act-Choice.why: Requiring the same $b$ passes the choice of thread $i$ to thread $j$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: j
args.meaning: The identifier of the partner thread, $j \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$ with $j \neq i$.

args.name: o
args.meaning: The selecting end, the partner branches on $\overline{o}$.

args.name: b
args.meaning: The choice, the same in both labels.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

args.name: f'
args.meaning: The term of thread $j$ after its step.

P-Act-Link.title: P-Act-Link
P-Act-Link.meaning: If $M(i) \xrightarrow{\leftrightarrow\{o_1, o_2\}} e'$ and $\mathsf{ech}\,o_1 \in C$, then $C$ loses $\mathsf{ech}\,o_1$ and every thread of $M[i \mapsto e']$ is renamed by $\mathsf{csub}\,o_1\,o_2$.
P-Act-Link.why: The label is unordered, so the rule applies with either end as $o_1$ and removes the channel of either end.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

P-Act-Session.title: P-Act-Session
P-Act-Session.meaning: If $M(i) \xrightarrow{\sigma} e'$ and $\mathsf{subj}\,\sigma \cap C = \varnothing$, then $(C, M) \to (C \setminus \mathsf{sentc}\,\sigma, M[i \mapsto e'])$, an offer to the environment.
P-Act-Session.why: A send of $v$ to the environment moves the ends $\mathsf{fends}(v)$, so their channels leave $C$. The process and the relation compute the extruded channels from the same $v$.
P-Act-Session.example: An external send of a restricted $d^{+}$ removes $d$ from $C$.

args.name: (C, M)
args.meaning: The configuration before the step, $C$ its restricted channels and $M$ its thread map.

args.name: i
args.meaning: The identifier of the acting thread, $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$.

args.name: \sigma
args.meaning: A session label with $\mathsf{subj}\,\sigma \cap C = \varnothing$, an offer to the environment.

args.name: e'
args.meaning: The term of thread $i$ after its step.

sem.sentc.title: $\mathsf{sentc}$
sem.sentc.why: These are the channels a message to the environment moves out of the process.

ev.event.title: Event
ev.event.meaning: $\mathsf{solo}_i\,\alpha\,k$ is a step of thread $i$ alone with thread label $\alpha$. $\mathsf{sync}_{i,j}\,\sigma$ is a step in which thread $i$ takes the send, close or select $\sigma$ on an end $o$ and thread $j$ the matching receive, close or branch on $\overline{o}$. $\mathsf{offer}_i\,\sigma$ is an offer of thread $i$ to the environment.
ev.event.why: Weak fairness asks of each thread $t$ that $t \in \mathsf{parts}(l_j)$ for some $j$, so every step names its threads.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: The thread label of a solo step.

args.name: k
args.meaning: The pick of a solo step.

args.name: \sigma
args.meaning: The session label of thread $i$, in a synchronization or an offer to the environment.

ev.pick.title: Pick $k$
ev.pick.meaning: What a process rule chooses beyond the thread label. $k = j$ names the new thread of a spawn. $k = (o_1, o_2)$ orders the ends of a link, so the channel of $o_1$ goes and the thread with $\overline{o_1}$ then holds $o_2$. Every other solo step has $k = \cdot$.
ev.pick.why: The thread label of a link is the unordered set $\{o_1, o_2\}$, and the thread label of a spawn names no thread, so the event records the choice the rule makes.

args.name: j
args.meaning: The identifier of a spawned thread.

args.name: o_1, o_2
args.meaning: The ends of a link, the channel of $o_1$ goes.

ev.admin.title: Administrative events
ev.admin.meaning: $\mathsf{admin}$ is the set of solo events $\mathsf{solo}_i\,\alpha\,k$, the steps by $\beta$, $\mathsf{new}$, $\mathsf{spawn}$ and $\mathsf{link}$, each of cost $0$ in $\kappa_L$.
ev.admin.why: They act on no protocol. Absence of internal divergence states that every chain of them is finite.
ev.admin.example: An unbounded chain of spawns takes only administrative steps.

ev.tau.title: $\tau$ events
ev.tau.meaning: Every event except $\mathsf{offer}_i\,\sigma$, an offer to the environment.
ev.tau.why: A closed configuration has no environment, so all its steps are $\tau$ steps.

prop.terminated.title: $\mathsf{terminated}$
prop.terminated.meaning: $\mathsf{terminated}\,p$ iff $p = (\varnothing, \{\!|v|\!\} \uplus E)$ with $v$ a value and $e = \ast$ for every $e \in E$.
prop.terminated.why: At the end $C = \varnothing$, so every channel is used up, and only the main thread returns a value.

args.name: v
args.meaning: The result of the main thread, a value.

args.name: E
args.meaning: The multiset of the other threads, each equal to $\ast$.

prop.df.title: $\mathsf{deadlock\_free}$
prop.df.meaning: $\mathsf{deadlock\_free}\,p$ iff for every $p'$ with $p \to^{*} p'$, $\mathsf{terminated}\,p'$ or $p' \to p''$ for some $p''$.
prop.df.why: It is the safety property the deadlock-freedom system proves of closed typed processes.

args.name: p'
args.meaning: Ranges over all processes with $p \to^{*} p'$.

prop.notau.title: $\mathsf{no\_tau\_divergence}$
prop.notau.meaning: For every $q$ with $p \to^{*} q$, $\mathsf{Acc}\ {\to_{\mathsf{admin}}}\ q$, so no infinite chain of administrative steps starts at $q$.
prop.notau.why: Lock freedom requires that a thread eventually performs its next action. An infinite chain of $\beta$, spawn or link steps never performs one.
prop.notau.breaks: $\mathsf{force}\,!(f = \mathsf{force}\,f)$ takes $\beta$ steps forever, and a forwarder that spawns a new forwarder at each round spawns forever.

args.name: q
args.meaning: Ranges over all processes with $p \to^{*} q$.

prop.padmin.title: Administrative step
prop.padmin.meaning: $q \to_{\mathsf{admin}} q'$ when $q \to q'$ with an administrative event.
prop.padmin.why: It is the relation that absence of internal divergence asks to be well-founded.

args.name: q, q'
args.meaning: Processes with $q \to q'$ by an event in $\mathsf{admin}$.

prop.lf.title: $\mathsf{lock\_free}$
prop.lf.meaning: For every run $(r, l)$ with $\mathsf{erase}(r_0) = p$ that is maximal and weakly fair, every thread $t$ pending at a position $i$ has $t \in \mathsf{parts}(l_j)$ for some $j \geq i$.
prop.lf.why: Deadlock freedom allows a thread to wait forever while other threads step. Lock freedom excludes it, and its definition mentions no type.
prop.lf.breaks: A server that serves one client forever while a second client waits is deadlock free and not lock free.

args.name: (r, l)
args.meaning: A run, $r_i \in \mathsf{Config}$ the configuration and $l_i$ the event or stutter at position $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

args.name: j
args.meaning: A position with $j \ge i$, existentially quantified.

prop.maximal.title: Maximal run
prop.maximal.meaning: For every $i$, either $r_i \to r_{i+1}$ by a $\tau$ event $l_i$, or $r_i$ has no $\tau$ step and $r_{i+1} = r_i$.
prop.maximal.why: A run that stutters while a step is possible would satisfy lock freedom vacuously, so the definition quantifies over maximal runs only.
prop.maximal.example: A run that stutters at $r_i$ while $r_i$ has a $\tau$ step is not maximal.

args.name: (r, l)
args.meaning: A run, $r_i \in \mathsf{Config}$ the configuration and $l_i$ the event or stutter at position $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

prop.wfair.title: Weak fairness
prop.wfair.meaning: For every position $i$ and thread $t$, there is $j \geq i$ with $t \in \mathsf{parts}(l_j)$ or $t$ disabled at $r_j$.
prop.wfair.why: Without fairness a scheduler may never run an enabled thread $t$, and no program with two threads is lock free.
prop.wfair.example: A run that never schedules an enabled thread is not weakly fair.

args.name: (r, l)
args.meaning: A run, $r_i \in \mathsf{Config}$ the configuration and $l_i$ the event or stutter at position $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

args.name: j
args.meaning: A position with $j \ge i$, existentially quantified.

prop.pend.title: Pending thread
prop.pend.meaning: $\mathsf{pend}(q, t)$ holds when thread $t$ of $q$ has a session label as its next step.
prop.pend.why: Lock freedom guarantees progress exactly to the pending threads.

prop.lfrun.title: $\mathsf{lf\_run}$
prop.lfrun.meaning: For every $i$ and $t$, $\mathsf{pend}(r_i, t)$ implies $t \in \mathsf{parts}(l_j)$ for some $j \geq i$.
prop.lfrun.why: It is the condition on one run, and $\mathsf{lock\_free}\,p$ asks it of every maximal weakly fair run from $p$.
prop.lfrun.example: Every message the client sends is received by the server at a later position.

args.name: (r, l)
args.meaning: A run, $r_i \in \mathsf{Config}$ the configuration and $l_i$ the event or stutter at position $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

args.name: i, t
args.meaning: Range over all positions and thread identifiers.

args.name: j
args.meaning: A position with $j \ge i$, existentially quantified.

ty.unit.title: Unit type $\ast$
ty.unit.meaning: The type of $\ast$, with $V\llbracket\Theta \vdash \ast\rrbracket = \{\ast\}$ at $\Theta = \varnothing$ and empty otherwise.
ty.unit.why: A plain type. $\mathsf{close}$, $\mathsf{link}$ and $\mathsf{spawn}$ return $\ast$, and every spawned thread returns $\ast$.

ty.arrow.title: Arrow
ty.arrow.meaning: \inmode{lf}{$(T \multimap^{u}_{l}\inmode{lf}{[c ; \vartheta]}\,U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ is a closure type with upper point $u$, lower point $l$, cost $c$, ticket need $\vartheta$\inmode{lf}{ and credit} $a$.} \inmode{lf}{The body sees each captured end at its own credit minus $a$.}
ty.arrow.why: A call runs code that may block and holds the ends of the closure. The type bounds where the call blocks by $u$ and where the held ends are by $l$.
ty.arrow.example: $\ast \multimap \ast$ is the type of a spawned thunk.

args.name: a
args.meaning: The credit of the captured ends above the floor $h$.

args.name: l
args.meaning: The lower point, absent iff the closure holds no end.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: A ticket need $(s, b)$ with $s, b \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, the function $r \mapsto 2^{s} r + b$ from tickets left to tickets needed.

args.name: h
args.meaning: The floor of the captured ends.

ty.ubound.title: Upper point $u$
ty.ubound.meaning: $u = x$ bounds the points where a call may block, $u = \cdot$ (no end held, nothing to bound) asks nothing of the caller, and $u = \top$ admits only the empty future, $\top \prec F \iff F = (\varnothing, \cdot)$.
ty.ubound.why: With $u = \top$ the body runs as the last code of its thread. A spawned abstraction is such a closure, so E-Abs at $u = \top$ and $l = \bot$ followed by E-Spawn types it, and V-Arrow at $(\top, \bot)$ is the predicate of a spawned thunk.

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 12.

ty.arrow.ub.title: Upper point $u$
ty.arrow.ub.meaning: The body is in $E$ under every $F$ with $\forall y \in F.\ u \prec y$, which every caller must establish.
ty.arrow.ub.why: The type of a closure does not show its body. The condition $u \prec F$ places the later actions of the caller above the points where the body may block.
ty.arrow.ub.breaks: Without $u$, a closure that blocks at $x$ with $y \prec x$ for some later action $y$ of the caller could be called first, and the thread waits on its own later action.
ty.arrow.ub.example: A function that blocks on an end at $\kappa$ has $u = \kappa$.

args.name: u
args.meaning: A point or absent. The body is in $E$ under every future $F$ with $u \prec y$ for all $y \in F$.

ty.arrow.lb.title: Lower point $l$
ty.arrow.lb.meaning: $\forall y \in \mathsf{ap}(\Theta).\ l \preceq y$ for the captured ends, with $l$ absent iff $\Theta = \varnothing$.
ty.arrow.lb.why: A closure is a held value. A thread blocked at $x$ while holding it needs $x \prec y$ for every dual point $y$ of the captured ends, and $x \prec l$ implies these facts.
ty.arrow.lb.breaks: Without $l$, a thread blocks at $x$ while it holds a closure with a captured end at $v$ and $x \not\prec \overline{v}$, so the partner of that end may wait on the thread.

args.name: l
args.meaning: A point with $l \preceq y$ for every dual point $y$ of the captured ends, or $\cdot$ iff the closure captures no end. Not $\bot$, which marks hidden points at $\exists^{\bot}$.

ty.arrow.cost.title: Arrow cost $c$
ty.arrow.cost.meaning: A call performs at most $c \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ channel actions before it returns.
ty.arrow.cost.why: A thread that holds an end $o$ while a call runs delays $o$ by at most $c$ actions. Aging subtracts $c$ from the credit of $o$.
ty.arrow.cost.breaks: A thread that holds an end across a call that never returns waits forever the partner. With $c = \infty$ the held end has credit $a - \infty$, which fails $c \leq a$ at finite counter bound.
ty.arrow.cost.example: A loop body that never returns has $c = \infty$.

args.name: c
args.meaning: An upper bound on the channel actions of one call before it returns.

ty.arrow.tix.title: ticket need $\vartheta$ of a call
ty.arrow.tix.meaning: A call that must leave its caller $r$ link tickets needs $\vartheta(r)$ tickets when it starts. With $\vartheta = (s, b)$, $\vartheta(r) = 2^{s} r + b$, where $s$ counts the spawns of the call, each of which halves the tickets of its thread, and $b$ covers its links.
ty.arrow.tix.why: A link acts on no protocol, so no counter of an end bounds how often a thread links. Each link uses one ticket of the linking thread and no step creates tickets, so every run performs finitely many links.
ty.arrow.tix.breaks: A thread that links the partner of a waiting end to a fresh channel in every round, and acts on some other channel in between, waits forever the waiting thread. Each round gives the waiting thread a fresh partner with a full counter, so counters never run out and only the tickets bound the rounds.
ty.arrow.tix.example: $\lambda x.\,\mathsf{link}\,x$ has $\vartheta = (0, 1)$ and needs $r + 1$ tickets. A body that spawns a child which links once has $\vartheta = (1, 1)$ and needs $2r + 1$, because the spawn halves the tickets.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: A ticket need $(s, b)$ with $s, b \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, the function $r \mapsto 2^{s} r + b$ from tickets left to tickets needed.

ty.arrow.floor.title: Floor $h$
ty.arrow.floor.meaning: Every captured end must have counter at least $h + a$ when the closure is built, and the body is typed with each captured end at credit $h$.
ty.arrow.floor.why: The counters of the captured ends at the time of a call are unknown when the body is typed. $h$ is the lower bound it may assume.

args.name: h
args.meaning: The credit of each captured end in the typing of the body.

ty.credit.title: Credit $a$
ty.credit.meaning: $a \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ on an end type $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ is a lower bound on the counter of that end. On a closure type $(T \multimap [\ldots ; h]\, U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ every captured end has counter at least $h + a$.
ty.credit.why: A counter bounds how many actions of other ends an end may still wait through. Only ends and closures hold ends of their own. A pair, a sum or an existential holds the ends of its parts, and their types have the credits.
ty.credit.breaks: A send of an end whose counter may be $0$ lets the end be sent on forever while its partner waits.

args.name: a
args.meaning: A lower bound on the counter of an end, or of the ends a closure captured above its floor.

ty.prod.title: Product
ty.prod.meaning: $T \otimes U$. Its value relation splits $\Theta = \Theta_1 \uplus \Theta_2$ between the components.
ty.prod.why: A plain type. $\mathsf{send}$ takes a pair and $\mathsf{recv}$ returns one.
ty.prod.example: $S_1@\iota \otimes S_2@\kappa$ for two ends of a client.

ty.sum.title: Sum
ty.sum.meaning: $T \oplus U$, the type of $\mathsf{inj}_1\,v$ with $v : T$ and of $\mathsf{inj}_2\,v$ with $v : U$.
ty.sum.why: A plain type. $\mathsf{branch}$ returns a sum whose injection records the choice.

args.name: T, U
args.meaning: The types of the two injections.

ty.sess.title: End type $S@x$
ty.sess.meaning: An end that runs the protocol $S$ and acts next at the point $x$.
ty.sess.why: The points order the next actions of all ends, and readiness compares them to exclude circular waiting.

args.name: x
args.meaning: The point of its next action.

args.name: a
args.meaning: Its credit, a lower bound on its counter.

ty.box.title: Box type
ty.box.meaning: $\Box(\forall\bar\iota\,\bar\alpha.\ C.\ \ast \multimap^{u} U)$ is a replicable thunk, usable at every point instance $\bar x$ with $C[\bar x]$ and every session instance $\bar s$.
ty.box.why: A loop needs fresh points in each round. Quantifying over $\bar\iota$ under $\Box$ gives every call its own instance.
ty.box.example: A client loop has type $\Box\forall\iota\,\kappa\,\zeta.\ C.\ \ast \multimap (S_1@\iota \otimes S_2@\kappa \multimap^{\zeta} \ast)$.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: $m$ point variables, instantiated at each $\mathsf{force}$ by points $\bar x$ with $C[\bar x]$.

args.name: C
args.meaning: The constraint over $\bar\iota$ and outer points.

args.name: u
args.meaning: The upper point of the thunk.

args.name: c, \vartheta
args.meaning: Cost and ticket need of one force.

ty.box.svars.title: Session variables $\bar\alpha$
ty.box.svars.meaning: $k$ session variables, instantiated at every $\mathsf{force}$ by session types whose recursion passes an action.
ty.box.svars.why: One box serves every protocol the caller substitutes for $\bar\alpha$.
ty.box.svars.example: A forwarder box for every protocol $\alpha$.

ty.box.constraint.title: Box constraint $C$
ty.box.constraint.meaning: A set of facts $x \prec y$ over $\bar\iota$ and outer points, possibly infinite.
ty.box.constraint.why: A loop orders the points of all its rounds at once, and an infinite $C$ states the facts of every round.
ty.box.constraint.breaks: Without $C$ a box cannot type a loop that waits on one end while it holds another across rounds.
ty.box.constraint.example: $C$ states $\iota \prec \overline{\kappa}$ for the points of every round of a client loop.

args.name: C
args.meaning: A set of facts over $\bar\iota$ and outer points, possibly infinite.

ty.ex.title: Existential
ty.ex.meaning: $\exists^{l}\bar\iota.\ C.\ T\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ is $T[\bar x]$ for some $\bar x$ with $C[\bar x]$, and $l$ bounds the dual points of its ends from below.
ty.ex.why: A fresh point is unknown outside the term that created the point. $\mathsf{new}$ returns an existential over it, and payloads bind their points the same way.

args.name: l
args.meaning: The lower bound, $\cdot$, $\bot$ or a point.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: $m$ point variables, the witness $\bar x$ is hidden.

ty.ex.lb.title: Lower bound $l$
ty.ex.lb.meaning: $l = \cdot$ when the value holds no end, $l = \bot$ when its ends are at points unknown outside, and $l = x$ when $x \preceq y$ for every dual point $y$ of its ends.
ty.ex.lb.why: $\bot$ stands for a fresh point that no fact of the context mentions, and $\mathsf{hbot}$ propagates $\bot$.
ty.ex.lb.breaks: Without $\bot$, a closure captures an unopened fresh pair and claims a lower point $l$ that no fact of $W$ supports.

args.name: l
args.meaning: $\cdot$ for no end, $\bot$ for ends at unknown points, $x$ when $x \preceq y$ for every dual point $y$ of the ends.

sty.skip.title: $\mathsf{Skip}$
sty.skip.meaning: The empty protocol, and an end at $S$ with $\mathsf{unfold}(S) = \mathsf{Skip}$ is idle.
sty.skip.why: No partner waits on an idle end. The fuel layer drops for idle ends the checks that counters are at least $1$, so they may be held indefinitely.
sty.skip.example: A control end that is passed around and never used is at $\mathsf{Skip}$.

sty.seq.title: Sequencing
sty.seq.meaning: $S.S'$ runs $S$ and then $S'$, and $\mathsf{unfold}$ normalizes it to its first action.
sty.seq.why: Sequencing composes protocols, so a recursion variable need not occur in tail position.

args.name: S, S'
args.meaning: The first and the second protocol.

sty.recv.title: Receive
sty.recv.meaning: $?(\bar\iota.\ T)$ receives a value of $T[x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)]$ for $\bar\iota = \iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$ when the end is at $x$.
sty.recv.why: A plain protocol action. The binder $\bar\iota$ is no existential, because the points of the payload are determined, the fields of $x$. It lets a message have ends whose points the receiver learns as fields of $x$.
sty.recv.example: $\mu\alpha.\,?(\kappa.\ \alpha @\kappa).\mathsf{Close}$ receives an end of the same protocol at a field.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: The point variables of the payload, $\iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$, placed at $x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)$ for the carrier point $x$.

sty.send.title: Send
sty.send.meaning: $!(\bar\iota.\ T)$ sends a value of $T[x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)]$ for $\bar\iota = \iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$. \inmode{lf}{The ends of $T$ have their credits, and the sender ages the payload by one transfer.}
sty.send.why: A plain protocol action, $\mathsf{dual}$ of receive.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: The point variables of the payload, placed at the fields of the carrier point.

sty.plus.title: Internal choice
sty.plus.meaning: $\oplus(S_1, S_2)$, where the selecting side chooses $i$ and continues with $S_1$ or $S_2$.
sty.plus.why: A plain protocol action. The holding thread decides the continuation.

sty.with.title: External choice
sty.with.meaning: $\&(S_1, S_2)$, where the branching side receives $i$ and continues with $S_1$ or $S_2$.
sty.with.why: A plain protocol action, $\mathsf{dual}$ of internal choice.

args.name: S_1, S_2
args.meaning: The continuations for the received $i = \mathsf{false}$ and $i = \mathsf{true}$.

sty.close.title: $\mathsf{Close}$
sty.close.meaning: The next action of the end is $\mathsf{close}$.
sty.close.why: A plain protocol action. Every finite protocol ends with $\mathsf{Close}$.

sty.mu.title: Recursion $\mu\alpha.S$
sty.mu.meaning: A recursive protocol, equal to its unrolling $S[\mu\alpha.S/\alpha]$ up to $\simeq$.
sty.mu.why: A plain former. Loops run repeating protocols.

sty.var.title: Session variable $\alpha$
sty.var.meaning: A recursion variable bound by $\mu$, or a session variable bound by a box.
sty.var.why: A plain former. It refers to an enclosing $\mu\alpha$ or to a protocol substituted at $\mathsf{force}$.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: A variable bound by an enclosing $\mu$ or by a box.

sty.vard.title: Dual variable $\overline{\alpha}$
sty.vard.why: The dual of a protocol substituted for $\alpha$ is known only after substitution, so $\overline{\alpha}$ defers the dual.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: A session variable, $\overline{\alpha}$ stands for $\mathsf{dual}$ of its instance.

sty.unfold.title: Head normal form
sty.unfold.meaning: $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ unrolls $\mu$ and reassociates sequencing until the first action is on top.
sty.unfold.why: Every rule reads the first action of a session type, so rules match on $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ and need no separate rule for $\mu$.

args.name: S
args.meaning: A contractive session type, $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ has its first action on top.

sty.dual.title: Duality
sty.dual.meaning: $\mathsf{dual}$ swaps $!$ with $?$ and $\oplus$ with $\&$, keeps payloads, $\mathsf{Skip}$ and $\mathsf{Close}$, and $\overline{S} := \mathsf{dual}\,S$.
sty.dual.why: The two ends of a channel run $S$ and $\mathsf{dual}\,S$, so every send meets a receive.

sty.flip.title: $\mathsf{flip}_\alpha$
sty.flip.meaning: $\mathsf{flip}_\alpha$ swaps $\alpha$ and $\overline{\alpha}$ for the variable bound by the enclosing $\mu$.
sty.flip.why: In $\mu\alpha.S$ the variable $\alpha$ names the whole protocol. After dualizing $S$, the occurrences $\overline{\alpha}$ must name $\mathsf{dual}(\mu\alpha.S)$, which is $\alpha$ again.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: The variable of the enclosing $\mu$, whose occurrences $\alpha$ and $\overline{\alpha}$ are swapped.

sty.sequiv.title: Session equivalence $\simeq$
sty.sequiv.meaning: The greatest relation with $S \simeq S'$ only if $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ and $\mathsf{unfold}(S')$ have the same first action, with equal annotations, and equivalent continuations.
sty.sequiv.why: One protocol has many spellings, unrolled or not. Rules compare protocols up to $\simeq$.

args.name: S, S'
args.meaning: Session types, related iff their unfoldings agree on first action and annotations and have related continuations.

ty2.stydf.title: $\mathsf{sty\_df}$
ty2.stydf.meaning: $\mathsf{sty\_df}(S)$ sets every annotation of $S$ to its value at $N = \infty$.
ty2.stydf.why: \inmode{lf}{Deadlock freedom and liveness read no credit, so two protocols that differ only in annotations are equal for them.}

sty.seqv.title: Up to annotations $\approx$
sty.seqv.why: \inmode{lf}{The relations of deadlock freedom and liveness ignore credits, so one relation serves every counter bound $N$.}

sty.sdual.title: Dual up to annotations
sty.sdual.why: The relation pairs the two ends of a channel by $\mathsf{sdual}$, consistent with comparing by $\approx$.
sty.sdual.example: A link of ends at $S$ and $S'$ asks $\mathsf{sdual}\,S\,S'$.

ty.heads.title: $\mathsf{ap}$
ty.heads.meaning: $\mathsf{ap}(T)$ is the set of dual points of the ends a value of $T$ holds. It is $\{\overline{x}\}$ for $S@x$, $\{l\}$ for an arrow or existential with bound $l$, and $\varnothing$ for bound $\cdot$. For $\otimes$ and $\oplus$ it is the union. An existential at $\bot$ contributes $\bot$.
ty.heads.why: A thread blocked at $u$ while holding a value of $T$ needs $u \prec y$ for every $y \in \mathsf{ap}(T)$, or the partner of a held end may wait on the thread. With $\bot$ in the set this fails, which is what hidden ends require.

ty.botord.title: $\bot$ in the order
ty.botord.meaning: No fact relates $\bot$ to a point, $\Gamma \nvdash x \prec \bot$ and $\Gamma \nvdash \bot \preccurlyeq y$.
ty.botord.why: Hidden ends are at points that no fact outside the existential mentions. A holding thread of such ends can be ordered against nothing, so it may not block.

ty.lbound.title: Lower bounds $l$
ty.lbound.meaning: $l ::= \cdot \mid \bot \mid x$, absent, unknown, or a point.
ty.lbound.why: It records which facts about the points of the hidden ends are available to a holding thread.

ty.payload-at.title: $\mathsf{payload\_at}$
ty.payload-at.why: $\overline{x}\cdot j = x\cdot j$, so sender at $x$ and receiver at $\overline{x}$ compute the same payload type.
ty.payload-at.example: A payload $\alpha @\iota_0$ sent at $Y$ has type $\alpha @Y\cdot 0$.

args.name: m
args.meaning: The number of point variables of the payload.

args.name: x
args.meaning: The point of the carrier end.

ty.pscoped.title: $\mathsf{pscoped}$
ty.pscoped.meaning: $\mathsf{pscoped}\,\bar\iota\,T$ iff every point variable of $T$ is among $\bar\iota$.
ty.pscoped.why: A payload mentions only its own point variables, so unrolling a $\mu$ never captures an outer point.
ty.pscoped.breaks: A free outer point inside a $\mu$-body is captured on unrolling, and point substitution changes its meaning.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: The point variables the payload binds.

ann.fuel.title: Numbers with $\infty$
ann.fuel.meaning: Credits, costs, floors, counters and the counter bound range over $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, where $\infty$ means unbounded and $\infty - c = \infty$.
ann.fuel.why: Deadlock-free typing sets every annotation to $\infty$. Then a held end remains arbitrarily many actions, and the checks on credits hold.

ann.tix.title: Ticket need $\vartheta$
ann.tix.meaning: A pair $\vartheta = (s, b)$ standing for the function $\vartheta(r) = 2^{s} r + b$. A term that must leave $r$ link tickets to the code after it needs $\vartheta(r)$ tickets when it starts. $b$ grows with the links of the term, $s$ counts its spawns, and $s = \infty$ means the term only runs if it leaves nothing.
ann.tix.why: Each link uses one ticket of its thread and each spawn transfers half of the tickets to the child. A pair $(s, b)$ describes every need these two operations produce, so the typing can compute needs by arithmetic.
ann.tix.breaks: Without a closed form the typing would need arbitrary functions from tickets to tickets.
ann.tix.example: $(0, 1)$ is one link, needing $r + 1$. $(1, 1)$ is a spawn whose child links once, needing $2r + 1$. $(0, \infty)$ is met by no ticket count.

args.name: r
args.meaning: The reserve of tickets on return.

ann.tid.title: No need $\hat 1$
ann.tid.meaning: $\hat 1 = (0, 0)$, the need of a term that performs no link and no spawn. It needs exactly the tickets it must leave, $\hat 1(r) = r$.
ann.tid.why: Values and most rules need nothing of their own.

ann.meets.title: $\vartheta(r) \leq tk$
ann.meets.meaning: $tk$ tickets cover the need $\vartheta$ with $r$ left over. It is false when $\vartheta(r) = \infty$.
ann.meets.why: A thread starts with finitely many tickets, and every link uses one.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: A ticket need $(s, b)$ with $s, b \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, the function $r \mapsto 2^{s} r + b$ from tickets left to tickets needed.

ann.tspawn.title: $\mathsf{tspawn}$
ann.tspawn.meaning: The need of a spawn followed by code of need $(s, b)$, when the child needs $b_c$, is $(s + 1, \max(2b, 2b_c - 1))$. The child receives $\lceil tk/2 \rceil$ of the $tk$ tickets and the parent keeps $\lfloor tk/2 \rfloor$. The parent must keep $\lfloor tk/2 \rfloor \geq 2^{s} r + b$, hence $tk \geq 2^{s+1} r + 2b$, and the child must get $\lceil tk/2 \rceil \geq b_c$, hence $tk \geq 2b_c - 1$. The pair is the larger of the two bounds.
ann.tspawn.why: Tickets belong to threads and a spawn creates a thread, so the child takes its tickets from the parent and no spawn creates any. Otherwise a loop that spawns a linking child in every round performs infinitely many links. The split is a fixed function of $tk$, the same in each run and at each step index. A split chosen freely could differ between indices, and the relation does not see how many tickets the child needs.
ann.tspawn.breaks: With fresh tickets for every child, a loop that spawns a child which links once, forever, is accepted, and a waiting thread whose partner is linked away in every round waits forever.
ann.tspawn.example: A thread spawns a child that links once and then links once itself. After the spawn the parent needs $(0, 1)$, one ticket, and the child needs $b_c = 1$. The start needs $\max(2 \cdot 1, 2 \cdot 1 - 1) = 2$ tickets, with $\lceil 2/2 \rceil = 1$ for the child and $\lfloor 2/2 \rfloor = 1$ for the parent, and $\mathsf{tspawn}\,1\,(0, 1) = (1, 2)$.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: The ticket need $(s, b)$ of the parent continuation.

ann.tlink.title: $\mathsf{tlink}$
ann.tlink.meaning: The need of a link followed by code of need $(s, b)$ is $(s, b + 1)$.
ann.tlink.why: The link uses one ticket before the rest runs. No step creates tickets, so a run performs at most as many links as its threads held tickets at the start.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: The ticket need $(s, b)$ after the link.

ann.tseq.title: Sequencing $\vartheta_1 \circ \vartheta_2$
ann.tseq.meaning: Code of need $\vartheta_1$ followed by code of need $\vartheta_2$ needs $\vartheta_1(\vartheta_2(r))$. The first part must leave what the second part needs.
ann.tseq.why: Application and the two lets run their parts one after the other.

args.name: \vartheta_1, \vartheta_2
args.meaning: The ticket needs of the first and the second part.

ann.tok.title: $\mathsf{tok}$
ann.tok.meaning: $\mathsf{tok}\,\vartheta_1\,\vartheta_2$ holds when $\vartheta_2$ needs nothing at $0$, $\vartheta_1$ has a finite $s$, or $\vartheta_1$ is met by no ticket count. Then the pair computed for $\vartheta_1 \circ \vartheta_2$ is exact.
ann.tok.why: With $s_1 = \infty$ the first part runs only if it leaves nothing, so a second part that needs tickets cannot follow. The rules that sequence two parts ask $\mathsf{tok}$.
ann.tok.example: $\mathsf{tok}\,(0, 1)\,(0, 1)$, the first need has a finite $s$.

ann.tydf.title: $\mathsf{ty\_df}$
ann.tydf.meaning: $\mathsf{ty\_df}(T)$ is $T$ with every annotation at its unbounded value. Credits, costs and floors become $\infty$ and every ticket need becomes $(\infty, \infty)$.
ann.tydf.why: Deadlock-free typing is the annotated typing at counter bound $N = \infty$ with these annotations. One set of rules then serves both systems, and every premise about annotations holds at $\infty$.

ty.unlimited.title: $\mathsf{unlimited}$
ty.unlimited.meaning: $\mathsf{unlimited}\,T$ iff $T$ is a box type, so its variables admit weakening and contraction.
ty.unlimited.why: $V$ at a box type asks $\Theta = \varnothing$, so copying or dropping the value duplicates or loses no end.
ty.unlimited.example: The self of a box is unlimited.

ty.tfree.title: $\mathsf{tfree}$
ty.tfree.meaning: $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$ iff $T$ is built from $\ast$, boxes, $\otimes$ and $\oplus$. A value of such a type holds no end, because $V$ at a box asks $\Theta = \varnothing$.
ty.tfree.why: Aging and capture leave an entry at a $\mathsf{tfree}$ type unchanged. P-Term asks it of the result, so no partner waits on the result of a process.
ty.tfree.breaks: A main thread that returns an end holds it forever, and its partner waits forever.

w.world.title: World
w.world.why: The order is an order on points, and $W$ is the data that generates the order $\prec_W$. A creation grows $W$ by its facts.

w.consts.title: Roots $A$
w.consts.meaning: $A$ is the finite set of roots of $W$.
w.consts.why: Facts mention only points with roots in $A$, and composition compares two worlds through $A_1 \cap A_2$.

w.facts.title: Facts $\prec_A$
w.facts.meaning: A set of facts $x \prec y$, possibly infinite, between points whose roots lie in $A$.
w.facts.why: They order the channels a component shares with its environment and the channels created so far.

w.lt.title: $\prec_W$
w.lt.meaning: $\prec_W$ is the transitive closure of the three generators, and $W \vdash x \prec y$ means $x \prec_W y$.
w.lt.why: A waiting chain combines several facts, so the order is transitive.

w.ws-fact.title: Facts generator
w.ws-fact.why: A plain generator. The facts of $W$ hold in $\prec_W$.

w.ws-po.title: $x \prec x^{+}$
w.ws-po.why: An end acts at $x$ before it acts at $x^{+}$, so $\prec_W$ contains the program order of each end.

ty2.le.title: Order or equal $\preceq$
ty2.le.why: Lower bounds compare by $\preceq$, so a closure whose only captured end has dual point $l$ may have lower point $l$.
ty2.le.example: A closure capturing $a^{+}$ at $\rho$ has $l = \overline{\rho}$ and $\overline{\rho} \preceq \overline{\rho}$.

w.ws-dpo.title: $x \prec \overline{x}^{+}$
w.ws-dpo.why: The fact holds in every run. The action at $x$ synchronizes with the partner at $\overline{x}$, and the partner acts at $\overline{x}^{+}$ only afterwards, so $W$ may contain it for free.

w.wf.title: $\mathsf{world\_wf}$
w.wf.meaning: $\mathsf{world\_wf}\,W$ iff every fact of $\prec_A$ relates points with roots in $A$.
w.wf.why: A fact outside $A$ mentions a point no component owns.
w.wf.example: A fact $1 \prec 3$ with $3 \notin A$ violates the property.

w.strict.title: $\mathsf{strict}$
w.strict.meaning: $\mathsf{strict}\,W$ iff $\mathsf{world\_wf}\,W$ and $W \nvdash x \prec x$ for every $x$, so $\prec_W$ is acyclic.
w.strict.why: Readiness of two threads that wait on each other needs $x \prec y$ and $y \prec x$, hence $x \prec x$. Strictness excludes such a cycle.
w.strict.breaks: In a cyclic $W$ two threads that wait on each other both count as ready, and a deadlocked process is in the relation.

w.lfworld.title: $\mathsf{wfworld}$
w.lfworld.meaning: $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$ iff $\prec_W$ is well-founded, so no infinite chain $\cdots \prec x_2 \prec x_1 \prec x_0$ exists.
w.lfworld.why: Lock freedom ranks a pending thread by the point of the end it waits on, and every waiting chain descends in $\prec_W$. Well-foundedness makes every such chain finite.
w.lfworld.breaks: Without it, waiting descends forever. Each thread waits on one below it, new threads keep appearing below, and the top thread never proceeds.

w.ext.title: Extension $\sqsubseteq$
w.ext.meaning: $W \sqsubseteq W'$ iff $A \subseteq A'$ and every fact of $W$ is a fact of $W'$.
w.ext.why: $W \sqsubseteq W'$ implies $\prec_W \subseteq \prec_{W'}$, so every relation stated monotone in $W$ remains growth and composition with another component.

args.name: W, W'
args.meaning: The smaller and the larger world.

w.grow.title: Growth $W \oplus C$
w.grow.meaning: $W \oplus C$ adds the roots of the facts $C$ to $A$ and the facts $C$ to $\prec_A$.
w.grow.why: A creation adds a fresh root and the facts its typing chose, so the world of a run grows with every $\mathsf{new}$ and never loses a fact.
w.grow.breaks: If the facts were fixed before the run, the facts of a fresh point would be chosen in advance. A channel between two given channels would then need these facts for each possible pair.
w.grow.example: $W \oplus \{1 \prec a,\ a \prec \overline{2}\}$ with $a$ fresh places $a$ between $1$ and $\overline{2}$.

args.name: C
args.meaning: The facts of a creation, over the fresh root and points of $W$.

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 2. The Rocq creates with new_ℓ and new_κ over generated roots.

w.join.title: Join $\sqcup$
w.join.meaning: $W_1 \sqcup W_2$ takes the unions of roots and facts.
w.join.why: Two components typed in $W_1$ and $W_2$ compose in $W_1 \sqcup W_2$.

w.restrict.title: Restriction $W|_S$
w.restrict.meaning: $W|_S$ has the facts $x \prec_W y$ with roots of $x, y$ in $S$.
w.restrict.why: It is the part of $\prec_W$ that is visible to another component through the shared constants $S$.

args.name: S
args.meaning: A set of constants, instantiated with $A_1 \cap A_2$.

w.R7.title: Strict join
w.R7.meaning: $\mathsf{strict}(W_1 \sqcup W_2)$ iff $\mathsf{strict}\,W_1$, $\mathsf{strict}\,W_2$ and $\mathsf{strict}(W_1|_S \sqcup W_2|_S)$ for $S = A_1 \cap A_2$.
w.R7.why: Strictness of the join is decided on the shared constants $S$ alone.
w.R7.example: Two strict worlds with $A_1 \cap A_2 = \varnothing$ have a strict join.

tj.Gamma.title: $\Gamma$, facts and future hypotheses
tj.Gamma.meaning: $\Gamma$ consists of a list of constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$ and a finite map of future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$, read as $u \prec \varphi$.
tj.Gamma.why: Every order fact a rule may use beyond $\prec_W$ is recorded in $\Gamma$. The derivable facts are exactly the judgments $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$.
tj.Gamma.example: In the body of the client loop $\Gamma$ holds $(C, [\iota, \kappa, \zeta])$.

args.name: (C, \bar x)
args.meaning: a constraint $C$ instantiated at the list of points $\bar x$

args.name: \varphi \mapsto u
args.meaning: a future variable $\varphi$ with the fact $u \prec \varphi$

tj.hage.title: $\mathsf{def}(H - c)$, aging what is held
tj.hage.meaning: $H - c$ ages every entry of $H$ by the cost $c$ of $e$. It is defined when every end and closure in $H$ that is not idle has credit at least $c$.
tj.hage.why: The thread holds $H$ while $e$ runs, and each of the up to $c$ actions of $e$ lowers the counters of the held ends by $1$.
tj.hage.breaks: Without it a thread holds an end across unboundedly many actions on other ends, and the partner of that end waits without bound.

args.name: H
args.meaning: the entries the thread holds while $e$ runs, a context or a type

lfi.credit.title: Credits, a bound on postponement
lfi.credit.meaning: Every end has a counter at run time, the number of actions the thread holding it may still perform on other ends before it must act on this one. The credit $a$ in $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ is a lower bound on that counter, known statically. A closure has a credit too, because the ends it captured are invisible in its type.
lfi.credit.why: A partner waiting on an end needs the holding thread to act on it eventually. If every action elsewhere lowers the counter and the counter must stay non-negative, the holding thread can only postpone the end finitely often.
lfi.credit.breaks: Postponement in the Examples tab holds $b$ across a loop that never returns, so $\mathsf{close}\,b'$ waits forever. The loop has cost $\infty$, and no credit is large enough.
lfi.credit.example: $(S@x)^{3}$ may be held across three actions on other ends.

args.name: a
args.meaning: a lower bound on the counter of the end, or of the ends a closure captured

lfi.cost.title: Cost, aging and counter bound, the counting
lfi.cost.meaning: The cost $c$ of a term bounds its actions before it returns. Every rule that runs a subterm while holding $\Delta$ ages $\Delta$ by that cost, $\Delta - c$, which asks each credit to be at least the cost. An action on an end counter bounds it to $N$, so the end returns as $(S@x^{+})\inmode{lf}{^{N}}$. Idle ends, $\mathsf{Skip}$, age without the check, because no thread waits on an idle end.
lfi.cost.why: Credits bound postponement only if the holding thread's actions lower the credits. The cost says how much, aging applies it to everything held, and the counter bound starts the count again after the holding thread kept its promise.
lfi.cost.breaks: Without the counter bound a long-running protocol would run out of credit after $N$ actions.
lfi.cost.example: $\langle c, \mathsf{send}\,\langle\ast, d\rangle\rangle$ ages $c$ by $1$ while the send on $d$ runs.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost, an upper bound on the actions of $e$

lfi.floor.title: Floors, credit inside a closure
lfi.floor.meaning: A closure $T \multimap[\varepsilon ; h]\, U$ records the floor $h$, the credit its body may assume of every captured end when it is called. At creation each captured end needs $h + a$, the floor plus what the closure itself may lose while it is held.
lfi.floor.why: Between creating a closure and calling it, the thread holding it may act elsewhere, which lowers the counters of the captured ends. The credit $a$ of the closure absorbs that loss, and $h$ is what remains for the body.
lfi.floor.breaks: Without the floor the body could not hold a captured end across any action.
lfi.floor.example: A callback with $h = 1$ and $a = 1$ needs its captured ends at credit $2$.

args.name: h
args.meaning: the credit the body may assume of every captured end

lfi.hop.title: Transfers, a passed end loses one
lfi.hop.meaning: Every time an end is transferred to another thread, by a send or a spawn, its counter drops by $1$. A send asks $T' - 1 \leq T[x\cdot i]$ of the payload, a spawned body sees $\Delta - 1$, and spawning a closure asks its credit $a \geq 1$.
lfi.hop.why: Transferring an end on is not an action on it, so it does not counter bound. Without the loss an end could be sent between threads forever and its partner would never be served.
lfi.hop.breaks: Endless delegation in the Examples tab sends $e$ back and forth forever while $e'$ waits. After finitely many transfers no credit is left to send it again.
lfi.hop.example: An end at credit $3$ can be passed on three times before a thread must act on the end.

args.name: T'
args.meaning: the type of a payload value

lfi.tickets.title: Tickets, a bound on links
lfi.tickets.meaning: Each thread holds a number of link tickets. A link uses one, and a spawn splits the tickets between parent and child. The ticket need $\vartheta$ of a term says how many tickets it needs, $\mathsf{tlink}$ adds one for a link and $\mathsf{tspawn}$ accounts for the split. P-Term asks the thread to start with enough.
lfi.tickets.why: A link acts on no end, so counters cannot bound the number of links. Worse, it gives the waiting thread a fresh dual end at full counter, so a thread could link forever while every counter stays full.
lfi.tickets.breaks: Link refresh in the Examples tab relinks the partner of a waiting end to a fresh channel every round, so the waiting thread always faces a new end. Each round uses a ticket and none is ever created.
lfi.tickets.example: A thread that links twice needs $\vartheta(0) \geq 2$.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: the ticket need, the tickets a term needs to leave $r$ behind

lfi.guard.title: The guard, no recursion before an action
lfi.guard.meaning: $\Lambda \vdash\!\triangleright t$ asks that a box calls itself only after a session action. It is a syntactic check on terms.
lfi.guard.why: Internal steps, $\beta$, $\mathsf{new}$ and $\mathsf{spawn}$, cost no counter. A loop made only of them would step forever without ever serving anyone, which deadlock freedom allows and lock freedom does not.
lfi.guard.breaks: Guard rejections in the Examples tab, e.g. $!(f = \mathsf{force}\,f)$ and a box that spawns itself forever.

args.name: \Lambda
args.meaning: the marks, which variables are boxes not yet allowed to recur

lfi.wf.title: A well-founded world
lfi.wf.meaning: $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$ asks $\prec_W$ to have no infinite descending chain. It is a premise of the lock-free theorems and no typing rule checks well-foundedness.
lfi.wf.why: A waiting thread waits on a holding thread whose own waiting point lies lower. With a well-founded order this chain ends, so someone at the bottom can act.
lfi.wf.breaks: A waiting chain that grows forever, in the Examples tab, spawns threads that each wait below their predecessor, and new ones keep appearing.
lfi.wf.example: Every world of the lock-free examples is well-founded.

tj.held.title: Holding $F \triangleleft H$
tj.held.meaning: $\Delta \vdash^{F \triangleleft H} e$ types $e$ while the thread holds $H$. The future $F \triangleleft H = F \cup \mathsf{ap}(H)$ adds the active points of $H$, \inmode{lf}{and in the lock-free mode the judgment also asks that $H - c$ is defined for the cost $c$ of $e$.}
tj.held.why: Every rule that runs one part while it holds another states the same facts about the held part, and the notation states them once. $H$ is a context, as in E-App, or a type, as in E-Pair.
tj.held.breaks: Without the future part a thread waits above an end it holds, and the partner of that end waits on the thread.

args.name: F \cup \mathsf{ap}(H)
args.meaning: $F$ with the dual points of the ends in $H$ added, and the flag $\bot$ added when $H$ holds an unopened existential at $\bot$

args.name: H
args.meaning: the entries the thread holds while $e$ runs, a context or a type

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of $e$, lock-free mode only

tj.eff.title: Effect $\varepsilon$
tj.eff.meaning: $\varepsilon = (c, \vartheta)$ pairs the cost $c$ of a term, an upper bound on its channel actions before it returns, with its ticket need $\vartheta$.
tj.eff.why: Cost and ticket need appear together and combine at the same places, so one symbol has both. Aging reads the cost, and the tickets of links read $\vartheta$.
tj.eff.example: A send has effect $\varepsilon \cdot 1$, one more action than its argument.

tj.seq.title: Sequencing $\varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2$
tj.seq.why: A term that runs two parts in sequence adds their costs and composes their ticket needs. The side condition $\mathsf{tok}$ becomes definedness, so no rule lists $\mathsf{tok}$.

args.name: \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2
args.meaning: the effects of the first and the second part

tj.zero.title: No effect $0$
tj.zero.why: A value performs no action and no link.

tj.one.title: One action $1$
tj.one.meaning: $1 = (1, \hat 1)$, the effect of one channel action.
tj.one.why: Every action adds one to the cost and needs no ticket.

tj.Delta.title: $\Delta$, the linear context
tj.Delta.meaning: $\Delta$ maps ends $o$ to end types $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ and de Bruijn indices $i$ to types $T$, with empty entries for indices another part owns.
tj.Delta.why: Ends and variables split the same way between two subterms, so one context holds both. A split puts an empty entry at index $i$ in the half that does not own variable $i$, so no index shifts.

args.name: o
args.meaning: an end held by the term, with its end type $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$

args.name: \Delta(i)
args.meaning: the entry of de Bruijn index $i$, empty or a type $T$

tj.F.title: The future $F$
tj.F.meaning: $F = (X, \varphi)$, $(X, \bot)$ or $(X, \cdot)$ with $X$ the points the context acts at after the term, $\varphi$ an unknown rest above a known point and $\bot$ a rest at hidden points.
tj.F.why: Every action at $x$ asks $x \prec F$. Hence a term never waits at a point above a point at which its own context still acts.
tj.F.breaks: Without $F$ the thread $\mathsf{let}\ \ast = \mathsf{close}\,c\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{close}\,d$ types for every placement of $c$ and $d$, and beside a partner that closes $d$ before $c$ both threads wait forever.

args.name: X
args.meaning: the finite set of points the context acts at after the term

args.name: \varphi
args.meaning: a future variable standing for an unknown set of points above its bound

args.name: \bot
args.meaning: the flag that the context holds ends at points unknown to the term

tj.W.title: The world $W$
tj.W.meaning: The world whose order $\prec_W$ the rules read.
tj.W.why: Every point fact a rule uses comes from $\prec_W$ or from $\Gamma$. Typing is monotone in $W$, so a program typed in $W$ is typed in every $W' \sqsupseteq W$.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world $(A, \prec_A)$ of roots and facts

tj.N.title: The counter bound $N$
tj.N.meaning: $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ is the credit of a fresh end and of an end after an action on that end.
tj.N.why: A credit is a lower bound on a counter, and each action of a holding thread on another end lowers the counter by $1$. A finite $N$ bounds the number of such actions between two actions on one end, which lock freedom needs, and $N = \infty$ gives deadlock-free typing.
tj.N.example: The client and server loop types at $N = 3$.

args.name: N
args.meaning: the credit of a fresh end and of an end after an action on it, $\infty$ for deadlock-free typing

ctx.tsplit.title: $\Theta = \Theta_1 \uplus \Theta_2$
ctx.tsplit.why: Each end has exactly one owner. Two subterms therefore never act on the same end.
ctx.tsplit.example: In E-App $\Theta_1$ holds the ends of $e_1$ and $\Theta_2$ those of $e_2$.

args.name: \Theta_1, \Theta_2
args.meaning: the ends given to the first and to the second subterm

ctx.lsplit.title: $\Delta = \Delta_1, \Delta_2$
ctx.lsplit.meaning: Every end of $\Delta$ goes to exactly one of $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$. For every index $i$, a linear entry goes to one side and the other side has an empty entry, and an entry of unlimited type goes to both.
ctx.lsplit.why: An end and a linear entry are used exactly once. An entry of unlimited type holds no end, so using it twice duplicates no end.
ctx.lsplit.example: A box variable $f$ may be forced in both $e_1$ and $e_2$.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context, ends $o$ with end types and de Bruijn indices with types

args.name: \Delta_1, \Delta_2
args.meaning: the contexts of the two subterms, the ends disjoint and the index lists of the same length as in $\Delta$

args.name: i
args.meaning: a de Bruijn index, linear entries go to one side, unlimited entries to both

ctx.hyps.title: Constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$
ctx.hyps.meaning: A constraint $C$ with the points $\bar x$ it is instantiated at, added by E-Box and E-Open.
ctx.hyps.why: A box body and the scope of an opened existential refer to their points only through these instances. The facts $C[\bar x]$ are the only hypotheses about these points.
ctx.hyps.example: $(C, [\iota, \kappa, \zeta])$ in the body of the client loop.

args.name: C
args.meaning: a box constraint, a set of facts over its bound point variables

args.name: \bar x
args.meaning: the points $C$ is instantiated at, fresh point variables $\bar\iota$ inside a box or an opened existential

ctx.fvar.title: Future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$
ctx.fvar.meaning: $\varphi \mapsto u \in \Gamma$ states $u \prec \varphi$ for an unknown future $\varphi$ above $u$.
ctx.fvar.why: A $\lambda$ or box body is typed once for all its callers. By E-App every caller future $F$ satisfies $u \prec F$, and $\varphi$ stands for every such $F$.

args.name: \varphi
args.meaning: a future variable naming the unknown future of a caller

args.name: u
args.meaning: the upper point of the closure or box, with $u \prec \varphi$

ctx.fvarF.title: The variable $\varphi$ in $F$
ctx.fvarF.meaning: The unknown part of a future, read only through $\Gamma \vdash u \prec \varphi$.
ctx.fvarF.why: In the semantics $\varphi$ denotes an arbitrary set of points above $u$. A body typed under $\varphi$ is therefore correct for every caller future above $u$.

args.name: \varphi
args.meaning: the variable part of the future

args.name: X
args.meaning: the known points of the future

ctx.bot.title: The flag $\bot$ in $F$
ctx.bot.meaning: $\bot$ states that the context holds ends at points unknown to the term, which then performs no session action.
ctx.bot.why: Every action asks $u \prec F$, which requires $F$ to have no $\bot$. No point is known to lie below a hidden point, so an action under $\bot$ could wait above the hidden point.
ctx.bot.example: $e_1$ beside a context that holds an unopened $\exists^{\bot}$.

args.name: \bot
args.meaning: the flag that some held end of the context has a point unknown to the term

args.name: X
args.meaning: the known points of the future

ctx.slt.title: $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$
ctx.slt.meaning: The least transitive relation containing $\prec_W$, the facts $C[\bar x]$ of the instances $(C, \bar x)$ in $\Gamma$, and $u \prec \varphi$ for every $\varphi \mapsto u$ in $\Gamma$.
ctx.slt.why: Every order fact a typing rule reads is a judgment $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$.

args.name: \Gamma
args.meaning: the hypotheses, constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$ and future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$

args.name: x, y
args.meaning: points, the judgment states that $x$ lies strictly below $y$

ctx.empty.title: $\Delta$ unlimited
ctx.empty.meaning: Every non-empty entry of $\Delta$ has unlimited type.
ctx.empty.why: A value that mentions no variable uses no linear entry, and an unlimited entry may go unused.
ctx.empty.example: $\ast$ types under every $\Delta$ whose entries are empty or unlimited.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context, ends $o$ with end types and de Bruijn indices with types

ctx.only.title: The only used entry
ctx.only.meaning: In $\Delta, x : T$ the entry $x$ is used and every entry of $\Delta$ has unlimited type.
ctx.only.why: Every linear entry is used exactly once, and an unlimited entry may go unused.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the rest of the context, unlimited

side.act.title: $x \prec F$ at an action
side.act.meaning: For an action at $x$ under $F = (X, \cdot)$, $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$ for every $y \in X$, $\Gamma \vdash x \prec \varphi$ when $F$ has a variable $\varphi$, and $F$ has no $\bot$.
side.act.why: While the term waits at $x$, every point at which its context acts later lies above $x$. This is readiness against the future.
side.act.breaks: Without it a term may wait at $x$ while its context must first act at a point below $x$, and the thread waits on itself through the dual end.
side.act.signature: x \prec F \iff (\forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \vdash x \prec y) \land (F = (X, \varphi) \Rightarrow \Gamma \vdash x \prec \varphi) \land F \neq (X, \bot)

args.name: x
args.meaning: the point of the end the action is on

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

args.name: \Gamma
args.meaning: the hypotheses, constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$ and future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$

act.refill.title: Credit $N$ after an action
act.refill.meaning: An end returned by an action, or created fresh, has credit $N$.
act.refill.why: The fuel layer sets the counter of an end to $N$ at every action on it, and the static credit is a lower bound on that counter.

args.name: S@x
args.meaning: the end after the action, at its new point

side.ub.title: $u \prec F$
side.ub.meaning: $u \prec F \iff (\forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \vdash u \prec y) \land \Gamma \vdash u \prec \varphi \land \bot \notin F$, true for absent $u$.
side.ub.why: It is the condition $x \prec F$ of an action, stated for the upper point $u$ up to which a callee may wait.
side.ub.example: E-App asks $u \prec F$ of the upper point $u$ of the closure.
side.ub.signature: u \prec F \iff (\forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \vdash u \prec y) \land (F = (X, \varphi) \Rightarrow \Gamma \vdash u \prec \varphi) \land F \neq (X, \bot)

args.name: u
args.meaning: the upper point of a closure or box, the highest point its body waits at

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

args.name: \Gamma
args.meaning: the hypotheses, constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$ and future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$

side.lb.title: $l \preccurlyeq H$
side.lb.meaning: $l \preccurlyeq H \iff \forall y \in H.\ l = y \lor \Gamma \vdash l \prec y$ for a point $l$, and $H = \varnothing$ for absent $l$.
side.lb.why: For a holding thread of a closure, the active points of its ends are bounded only through $l$. Hence $l$ must be a lower bound of those active points.
side.lb.signature: l \preccurlyeq H \iff (l = \cdot \Rightarrow H = \varnothing) \land \forall y \in H.\ l = y \lor \Gamma \vdash l \prec y

args.name: l
args.meaning: a lower point, or $\cdot$ when the value holds no end

args.name: H
args.meaning: a set of active points, dual points of held ends

side.hold.title: $\Gamma \vdash C[\bar x]$
side.hold.meaning: For every fact $y \prec z$ of $C$ instantiated at $\bar x$, $\Gamma \vdash y \prec z$.
side.hold.why: E-Force and E-Pack choose an instance $\bar x$, and the box body or the packed value relies on $C[\bar x]$.
side.hold.example: The self call of the client loop instantiates $C$ at $(\iota^{+}, \kappa^{+}, \zeta)$.
side.hold.signature: \Gamma \vdash C[\bar x] \iff \forall (y \prec z) \in C[\bar x].\ \Gamma \vdash y \prec z

args.name: \bar x
args.meaning: a list of $m$ points, the instance

args.name: \Gamma
args.meaning: the hypotheses, constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$ and future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$

age.free.title: Aging a type without ends
age.free.why: A type without ends has no counter that could fall, so aging changes nothing.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs meanwhile

age.credit.title: Aging an end or a closure
age.credit.meaning: $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = (S@x)^{a - c}$ and $(T \multimap U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = (T \multimap U)^{a - c}$, defined when $c \leq a$.
age.credit.why: While a term of cost $c$ runs, the holding thread performs up to $c$ actions on other ends, and each lowers the counter of every held end by $1$. The premise $c \leq a$ keeps the credit a lower bound on the counter.
age.credit.breaks: Without $c \leq a$ a server holds its client end while it runs a callback of cost $\infty$ at finite $N$, and the client waits without bound.

args.name: a
args.meaning: the credit of the end or closure

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs while it is held

age.idle.title: Aging an idle end
age.idle.why: No thread acts on an idle end, so no action counter bounds an idle end. Truncation keeps its credit at or below its counter, which decrements and truncates at $0$ in the same way.
age.idle.breaks: With $c \leq a$ required an idle end held across a loop loses credit every round and no finite $N$ types the loop. Keeping the credit instead exceeds the counter after one decrement.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs while the end is held

age.agg.title: Aging a product, sum or existential
age.agg.meaning: Aging goes into the parts. $(T_1 \otimes T_2) - c = (T_1 - c) \otimes (T_2 - c)$, likewise for $\oplus$, and $\exists^{l}\bar\iota.\,C.\,T$ ages its body.
age.agg.why: Only ends and closures have credits, so a compound type ages by aging the ends and closures it contains.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs while the value is held

age.ctx.title: Aging what is held
age.ctx.meaning: $\Delta - \varepsilon$ ages every entry of $\Delta$ by the cost $c$ of $\varepsilon = (c, \vartheta)$.
age.ctx.why: The entries are held while the subterm with effect $\varepsilon$ runs, and each of its actions lowers their counters by $1$.
age.ctx.breaks: Without aging a thread holds an end across unboundedly many actions on other ends, and the partner of that end waits without bound.
age.ctx.example: In the cycle example main loses $1$ of the credit of $d$ while it closes $c$.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the entries held while a subterm runs

args.name: \varepsilon = (c, \vartheta)
args.meaning: the effect of that subterm, whose cost $c$ ages every entry

cap.sess.title: Capturing an end
cap.sess.why: The closure itself has credit $a$ and ages by up to $a$ before its body runs. The body may assume credit $h$ on the end, so the end needs $h + a$.

args.name: h
args.meaning: the floor of the closure, the credit its body may assume of every captured end

args.name: a_0
args.meaning: the credit of the captured end

cap.arr.title: Capturing a closure
cap.arr.meaning: $(T \multimap[\varepsilon;h_0] U)\inmode{lf}{^{a_0}} \leadsto_{h,a} (T \multimap[\varepsilon;h_0] U)^{h - h_0}$, defined when $h_0 \leq h$ and $h + a \leq h_0 + a_0$.
cap.arr.why: A captured closure guarantees credit $h_0 + a_0$ on its own ends, and the premise asks this to cover $h + a$. The new credit $h - h_0$ places those ends at exactly the floor $h$ of the outer closure.
cap.arr.example: A callback with $h_0 = 1$ and $a_0 = 2$, captured at $h = 2$ and $a = 1$, gets credit $1$.
cap.arr.signature: h_0 \leq h \land h + a \leq h_0 + a_0 \Rightarrow (T \multimap[\varepsilon;h_0] U)\inmode{lf}{^{a_0}} \leadsto_{h,a} (T \multimap[\varepsilon;h_0] U)^{h - h_0}

args.name: h_0
args.meaning: the floor of the captured closure

args.name: h, a
args.meaning: the floor and credit of the capturing closure

cap.agg.title: Capture of other types
cap.agg.meaning: Capture goes into the parts of $\otimes$, $\oplus$ and $\exists$ and leaves types with $\mathsf{tfree}$ unchanged.
cap.agg.why: Only ends and closures have credits, so only they are restated.

args.name: h, a
args.meaning: the floor and credit of the capturing closure

sub.tsub.title: Subtyping $T \leq T'$
sub.tsub.meaning: The least relation closed under Sub-Sess, Sub-Arr, Sub-Box, Sub-Ex and componentwise on $\otimes$ and $\oplus$, used by E-Sub.
sub.tsub.why: The branches of $\mathsf{case}$ and of a received choice need one common type. Every clause weakens what a value guarantees.
sub.tsub.breaks: Without E-Sub two branches that create a channel with different facts have no common result type.

args.name: T'
args.meaning: the type it is used at

tp.sub-credit.title: Credits may fall
tp.sub-credit.meaning: $a' \leq a$ for the credits of an end.
tp.sub-credit.why: A credit is a lower bound on the counter of an end, so a smaller credit guarantees less. $\mathsf{new}$ and every action return credit $N$, and a parameter or a payload asks a fixed credit $b \leq N$.
tp.sub-credit.breaks: Without it a fresh end at credit $N$ fits only a parameter at credit exactly $N$, and no loop that ages an end before its self call types.

args.name: a
args.meaning: the credit of the end in the subtype

tp.sub-floor.title: The wait bound of an arrow
tp.sub-floor.meaning: $h \leq h'$ and $h' + a' \leq h + a$ for the floors $h, h'$ and credits $a, a'$ of two arrows.
tp.sub-floor.why: The body of a closure may assume that every captured end has credit $h$, and the holding thread guarantees $h + a$ in total. Raising the floor to $h'$ is sound only when the guarantee $h' + a'$ does not exceed the old $h + a$.
tp.sub-floor.breaks: Without $h' + a' \leq h + a$ a closure could claim a floor above the credit its captured ends have.
tp.sub-floor.signature: h \leq h' \land h' + a' \leq h + a

args.name: h, a
args.meaning: floor and credit of the arrow subtype

args.name: h', a'
args.meaning: floor and credit of the arrow supertype

tp.sub-sess.title: Session types up to equivalence
tp.sub-sess.meaning: $S \simeq S'$, bisimilar head normal forms with equal annotations, which is $S \approx S'$ at annotations $\infty$.
tp.sub-sess.why: With $\mathsf{Skip}$, sequencing and $\mu$ one protocol has many spellings, e.g. $\mathsf{Skip}.S \simeq S$. Rules compare protocols by behaviour.
tp.sub-sess.breaks: Without it an unfolded recursive protocol and its folded form would be different types, and no loop that acts once and recurses would type.

args.name: S, S'
args.meaning: session types at the same point $x$

tp.sub-ex.title: An existential may drop facts
tp.sub-ex.meaning: $\mathsf{facts}\,C' \subseteq \mathsf{facts}\,C$, the constraint $C'$ of the supertype states a subset of the facts of $C$ over the same variables.
tp.sub-ex.why: E-New states the facts $C$ of a creation in its existential. Two branches of a $\mathsf{case}$ or two creations that serve one type then agree on the facts both state, by dropping the rest.
tp.sub-ex.breaks: Without it, two branches that create a channel with different facts have different result types, and the $\mathsf{case}$ does not type.

args.name: C
args.meaning: the constraint of the subtype existential

args.name: C'
args.meaning: the constraint of the supertype existential, over the same variables

tp.sub-var.title: Variance
tp.sub-var.meaning: $\leq$ is contravariant in the argument and covariant in the result of $\multimap$, and covariant in the components of $\otimes$ and $\oplus$.
tp.sub-var.why: A closure that accepts more and returns less can stand for one that accepts less and returns more.

tp.sub-agg.title: Products and sums
tp.sub-agg.meaning: $T_1 \otimes T_2 \leq T_1' \otimes T_2'$ when $T_i \leq T_i'$ for $i = 1, 2$, and likewise for $\oplus$.
tp.sub-agg.why: \inmode{lf}{A product or a sum has no credit of its own, so it compares part by part.}

args.name: T_i, T_i'
args.meaning: the components of the two products or sums

tp.sub-teq.title: Equal up to $\simeq$
tp.sub-teq.meaning: $T \equiv T'$, the two types have the same shape and their session types are pairwise $\simeq$.
tp.sub-teq.why: The body of a box and of an existential is compared exactly up to protocol spellings. \inmode{lf}{Credits inside it are not lowered, because a box is copied and an existential is opened at its own credit.}

args.name: T, T'
args.meaning: types of the same shape whose session types are pairwise $\simeq$

E-Abs.phi.title: Fresh future variable
E-Abs.phi.meaning: The body is typed under $(\varnothing, \varphi)$ for a $\varphi \notin \mathrm{dom}\,\Gamma$ with $u \prec \varphi$.
E-Abs.phi.why: The body runs when a caller applies the closure, and by E-App every caller future $F$ satisfies $u \prec F$. Typing under a fresh $\varphi$ covers all such $F$.
E-Abs.phi.breaks: A body typed under the future of its definition is checked against facts that fail at another call site.
E-Abs.phi.example: The body of $\mathsf{between}$ runs under $\varphi$ with $\kappa \prec \varphi$.

args.name: \varphi
args.meaning: the future variable of the body

args.name: \Gamma
args.meaning: the hypotheses, constraint instances $(C, \bar x)$ and future variables $\varphi \mapsto u$

E-Abs.lb.title: Lower point of a closure
E-Abs.lb.meaning: $l \neq \bot \Rightarrow l \preccurlyeq \Delta$. A point $l$ lies at or below every element of $\mathsf{ap}(\Delta)$, and $l = \bot$ claims no bound.
E-Abs.lb.why: A thread holding the closure reads the dual points of its ends only through $l$. A closure at $l = \bot$ puts $\bot$ into the future of the thread holding it, so that thread may not wait while it holds the closure, as for $\exists^{\bot}$.
E-Abs.lb.breaks: A thread holding ends at the unrelated points $1$ and $2$ has no common lower point. A $\lambda$ that captures both types at $l = \bot$ and can then only be spawned or called in tail position.

args.name: l
args.meaning: the lower point of the arrow

args.name: \mathsf{ap}(\Delta)
args.meaning: the dual points of every captured end, with $\bot$ for hidden ends

E-Abs.cap.title: Capture as aging
E-Abs.cap.meaning: \inmode{lf}{The body of a closure\inmode{lf}{ at credit $a$} sees $\Delta - a$, each captured end and closure at its own credit minus $a$.}
E-Abs.cap.why: The thread holding the closure performs up to $a$ actions before the call. \inmode{lf}{The body may therefore assume each captured credit minus $a$.} \inmode{lf}{Each end keeps its own credit, so an end at $N$ captured next to an end at $1$ stays at $N - a$.}
E-Abs.cap.breaks: \inmode{lf}{With one floor for every captured end, an end at $N$ captured next to an end at $1$ drops to $0$.} A child that acts on the second end while it holds the first then has no typing.
E-Abs.cap.example: $a^{+}$\inmode{lf}{ at credit $3$} in a closure\inmode{lf}{ at credit $1$} is seen\inmode{lf}{ at credit $2$}.

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 12.

E-Abs.fut.title: Future of the body
E-Abs.fut.meaning: For $u \neq \top$ the body runs under a fresh variable $\varphi$ with the hypothesis $u \prec \varphi$. For $u = \top$ it runs under the empty future $(\varnothing, \cdot)$.
E-Abs.fut.why: A caller applies the closure only under a future $F$ with $u \prec F$, and $\top \prec F$ holds only for the empty future, so a closure at $\top$ is the last code of its thread.
E-Abs.fut.example: $\lambda e : \ast \multimap^{\top}_{\bot} \ast$ for a thunk that is spawned.

args.name: u
args.meaning: the upper point of the arrow

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 12.

side.top.title: $\top \prec F$
side.top.meaning: $\top \prec F$ holds exactly for the empty future $F = (\varnothing, \cdot)$.
side.top.why: The upper point $\top$ lies above every point, so nothing may follow a call of such a closure. E-Spawn runs it as a new thread, where nothing follows.
side.top.example: E-App with $u = \top$ needs $F = (\varnothing, \cdot)$, a call in tail position of a thread.

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 12.

E-Abs.body.title: Body of a $\lambda$
E-Abs.body.meaning: $e$ is typed under $\Gamma$ extended by $u \prec \varphi$, the captured $\Delta$ extended by the argument $T$, and the future $(\varnothing, \varphi)$. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode the captured entries are restated at the floor $h$.}
E-Abs.body.why: The body runs at a later call. It may rely only on its captured entries, its argument and $u \prec \varphi$, and E-App establishes $u \prec F$ at every call.
E-Abs.body.example: The body of the client loop with argument $S_1@\iota \otimes S_2@\kappa$.

args.name: \varepsilon
args.meaning: the effect recorded on the arrow

E-App.ub.title: $u \prec F$ at a call
E-App.ub.meaning: The upper point $u$ of the closure satisfies $u \prec F$.
E-App.ub.why: The callee waits only at points up to $u$. Every point at which the caller acts afterwards lies above $u$.
E-App.ub.breaks: A call of a closure that waits at $\kappa$, while the caller must still act at a point below $\kappa$, makes the caller wait on itself.

args.name: u
args.meaning: the upper point of the arrow type of $e_1$

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

E-App.fut1.title: The first subterm runs while the rest is held
E-App.fut1.meaning: $e_1$ is typed at the future $F \triangleleft \Delta_2$, which is $F \cup \mathsf{ap}(\Delta_2)$, with $\bot$ added when $\Delta_2$ has $\bot$.
E-App.fut1.why: The entries of the second subterm are held while $e_1$ runs. Hence $e_1$ must not wait above their dual points.
E-App.fut1.breaks: $\mathsf{let}\ \ast = \mathsf{close}\,c\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{close}\,d$ beside a partner that closes $d$ before $c$ deadlocks. E-LetU rejects the first thread unless $x_c \prec \overline{x_d}$.
E-App.fut1.example: The cycle example needs $\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}$ for $\mathsf{close}\,c$ while $d$ is held.

args.name: \Delta_1
args.meaning: the part of the context given to $e_1$

args.name: \Delta_2
args.meaning: the part held for the rest of the term

E-App.fut2.title: The argument runs while the closure is held
E-App.fut2.meaning: $e_2$ is typed while the thread holds the closure, so its future is $F \cup \{l\}$ with $l$ the lower point of the closure. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode the closure ages by the cost of $e_2$, which needs that much credit.}
E-App.fut2.why: The closure is held while $e_2$ runs, and $l$ bounds the dual points of its ends from below.

args.name: l
args.meaning: the lower point of the closure, held while $e_2$ runs

args.name: a
args.meaning: the credit of the closure, which bounds the cost of $e_2$

E-Pair.fut2.title: The second component runs while the first is held
E-Pair.fut2.meaning: $e_2$ is typed while the thread holds the value of $e_1$, so its future is $F \cup \mathsf{ap}(T_1)$. In the lock-free mode $T_1$ ages by the cost of $e_2$.
E-Pair.fut2.why: The value of $e_1$ is held while $e_2$ runs.

args.name: T_1
args.meaning: the type of the first component, held while $e_2$ runs

tp.letp.title: Body of a pair elimination
tp.letp.meaning: $e_2$ is typed under $\Delta_2$, aged by $e_1$ in the lock-free mode, extended by $T_2$ at index $0$ and $T_1$ at index $1$, under $F$.
tp.letp.example: $\mathsf{let}\ \langle v, c\rangle = \mathsf{recv}\,c\ \mathsf{in}\ e$ binds the received value and the continuation end.

tp.letu.title: Body of a unit elimination
tp.letu.meaning: $e_2$ is typed under $\Delta_2$, aged by $e_1$ in the lock-free mode, under $F$, after $e_1$ returned $\ast$.
tp.letu.why: $\ast$ holds no end, so nothing is bound. The rule sequences $e_1$ before $e_2$.

args.name: \Delta_2 - \varepsilon_1
args.meaning: the context of $e_2$ aged by the cost of $e_1$

E-Case.branches.title: Branches
E-Case.branches.meaning: Each branch $e_i$ is typed under $T_i, \Delta_2$ at the common result $T$.
E-Case.branches.why: Exactly one branch runs, and the choice is known only at run time. Both branches must fit the same continuation.

args.name: T_i
args.meaning: the payload of injection $i$ at index $0$

E-Box.unl.title: $\Delta$ unlimited
E-Box.unl.meaning: Every entry of $\Delta$ has unlimited type, so $\Delta$ holds no end.
E-Box.unl.why: A box value is copied freely. If it held an end, a copy would duplicate that end.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context, ends $o$ with end types and de Bruijn indices with types

E-Box.inst.title: Typed for every instance
E-Box.inst.meaning: The premise has one derivation of the body for every list $\bar s$ with $\mathsf{sinsts}\,\bar s$, one session type per session variable $\bar\alpha$ of the box.
E-Box.inst.why: A force may pick any allowed $\bar s$, and the derivation for that $\bar s$ is the one that justifies the call. Checking every instance up front keeps E-Force a plain lookup.
E-Box.inst.example: A box with no session variable has exactly one instance, the empty list, so the premise is one derivation.

args.name: \bar s
args.meaning: a list of session types, one per session variable of the box

E-Box.body.title: Body of a box
