F-Send.payload.why: $FV$ reads no point, so the raw payload type and its placed form agree.
F-Send.payload.example: $FV^N_n\llbracket \{a \mapsto S^{2}\} \vdash (S@x)^{2}\rrbracket$ for a payload end promised at credit $2$.

F-Recv.title: F-Recv
F-Recv.meaning: An action on $o$ that continues for every incoming value in $FV$ at every level $j \leq n$ with ends disjoint from $\Phi$.
F-Recv.why: The receiver continues for every value its type admits, and the lock-free process relation supplies the sender's transferred ends.

args.name: j, \Phi_i
args.meaning: its level and the ends it brings

F-Recv.forall.title: Every incoming value
F-Recv.forall.why: Every value in $FV$ is exact, so incoming closures hold exactly what they mention.
F-Recv.forall.breaks: Without exactness, a received closure owning nothing but mentioning an end could not be spawned.

args.name: \Phi_i
args.meaning: the ends of the received value, disjoint from $\Phi$

F-Close.title: F-Close, F-Select, F-Branch
F-Close.meaning: Actions that drop $o$ and decrement the rest at a close, or advance the protocol of $o$ to $S_i$ and set it back to $N$ at a choice.
F-Close.why: They are the fuel forms of O-Close, O-Select and O-Branch, and each is an action, so F-Count applies.

args.name: i
args.meaning: the choice, for select and branch

F-Link.title: F-Link
F-Link.meaning: Two distinct held ends at dual protocols leave, and one ticket is used.
F-Link.why: Tickets bound the links between actions.

F-Link.plink.title: Dual held ends
F-Link.plink.meaning: $o_1 \neq o_2$, both held, at protocols $S$ and $S' \simeq \overline{S}$, with annotations.
F-Link.plink.why: After the link the partners form one channel, whose protocols are dual only if the two linked protocols were, and annotations must match for later payload credits.
F-Link.plink.breaks: A credit mismatch at a link breaks the payload credit of a later message.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, a finite map $o \mapsto S^{f}$ from ends to a protocol and a counter $f \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

F-Link.ticket.title: $1 \leq tk$
F-Link.ticket.why: Tickets are conserved and used, so links cannot repeat forever.
F-Link.ticket.breaks: A box that links once per round forever.

FV-Sess.title: $FV$ at $S@x$
FV-Sess.meaning: An end with protocol $S' \simeq S$ and counter $f \geq a$.
FV-Sess.why: Credits are lower bounds on counters.

args.name: S@x, a
args.meaning: the end type and its credit

FV-Sess.counter.title: $a \leq f$
FV-Sess.counter.why: Typing reasons with credits and the lock-free process relation with counters, and this inequality transfers every credit bound of typing to the counters.
FV-Sess.counter.breaks: Without it, a context could age an end below its actual counter and F-Count would fail on an end whose credit typing treats as positive.

FV-Arrow.title: $FV$ at an arrow
FV-Arrow.meaning: A closure whose body has fuel for every larger counter bound, lower level, counters at or above the floor and argument in $FV$.
FV-Arrow.why: The clause reads costs, ticket needs, floors and credits, the data typing attaches to arrows.

args.name: c, \vartheta, h
args.meaning: the cost, ticket need and floor of the arrow

FV-Arrow.exact.title: $\mathsf{fends}\,e = \mathrm{dom}\,\Phi$
FV-Arrow.exact.meaning: The closure holds exactly the ends it mentions.
FV-Arrow.exact.why: It mirrors exactness of $V$, and the cost fundamental theorem needs it to read fuel off typing.
FV-Arrow.exact.breaks: A closure mentioning an end it does not hold would be in $FV$, and a forwarder receiving that closure could not spawn the closure.

FV-Arrow.floor.title: Counters $\geq a$
FV-Arrow.floor.meaning: Every captured counter $f$ of an end that is not idle has $a \leq f$.
FV-Arrow.floor.why: The closure's credit $a$ is a lower bound on each captured counter, as the credit of an end is on its own counter.

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 12.

FV-Arrow.body.title: Body fuel
FV-Arrow.body.meaning: $e[u] \in F^{N'}_j\llbracket\Phi' \cup \Phi_u ; tk \vdash U\ !\ (c, r)\rrbracket$ for every $tk$ with $\vartheta(r) \leq tk$.
FV-Arrow.body.why: The caller supplies an argument, counters lowered to the floor by its own actions, and a ticket count covering the arrow's ticket need, and the body guarantees fuel with frame $c$.

args.name: N', j
args.meaning: a larger counter bound and a lower level

args.name: \Phi'
args.meaning: the captured ends with counters at the call, at least $h$

FV-Box.title: $FV$ at a box
FV-Box.meaning: A box with no ends whose body has fuel per force at every larger counter bound, lower level and session instance in $\mathsf{sinsts}\,N'$.
FV-Box.why: A box is unlimited, so it holds no counters and works at every use.

FV-Box.noends.title: $\mathsf{fends}\,e = \varnothing$
FV-Box.noends.meaning: A box mentions no end and holds no protocol or counter.
FV-Box.noends.why: A copied box would otherwise copy ends.

FV-Box.body.title: Body per force
FV-Box.body.meaning: $e[!e] \in F^{N'}_j\llbracket\varnothing ; tk \vdash U[\bar s]\ !\ (c, r)\rrbracket$ for every $N' \sqsupseteq_{\mathsf{rle}} N$, $j < n$, $\bar s \in \mathsf{sinsts}\,N'$ and $tk \geq \vartheta(r)$.
FV-Box.body.why: Each force unrolls the box once, at a counter bound and instance the forcing context chooses.
FV-Box.body.signature: e[!e] \in F^{N'}_{j}\llbracket \varnothing ; tk \vdash U[\bar s]\ !\ (c, r) \rrbracket

args.name: N', j
args.meaning: a larger counter bound and a lower level

FV-Thread.title: Thread result
FV-Thread.why: A finished thread holds no end.

fu.fsem.title: $\mathsf{fsem}$
fu.fsem.meaning: $\mathsf{fsem}\,N\,\Phi\,e \iff \exists tk.\ \forall n.\ e \in F^N_n\llbracket\Phi ; tk \vdash \mathsf{thread}\ !\ (\infty, 0)\rrbracket$, where each counter of $\Phi$ is $N$.
fu.fsem.why: It is the fuel of a thread that the lock-free process relation requires, and the cost fundamental theorem derives it from typing. It is the one fuel statement that holds at every level.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, a finite map $o \mapsto S^{f}$ from ends to a protocol and a counter $f \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

args.name: tk
args.meaning: the ticket count, fixed for all levels

cs.csem.title: $\Delta \vDash^{N} e : T\ !\ \varepsilon$
cs.csem.meaning: For every larger counter bound, level, injective renaming of the ends of $\Delta$, grounding in $FV$ and ticket count meeting $\vartheta$, the instance has fuel at $T$ with frame $c$, for $\varepsilon = (c, \vartheta)$.
cs.csem.why: It reads no $\Gamma$, world or future, because fuel reads none of these.
cs.csem.example: The cost fundamental theorem concludes this judgment.

args.name: \varepsilon
args.meaning: the effect, cost and ticket need

sp.state.title: Annotated configuration $a = (q, K, tk)$
sp.state.meaning: A configuration $q$, an ownership map $K$ and a ticket count per thread.
sp.state.why: Ranks and counters of the termination measure are read off $K$, so ownership is fixed outside the index.
sp.state.breaks: Placement chosen per level lets a waiting main thread wait forever in every fair run.

args.name: K
args.meaning: the ownership map of the annotated configuration

sp.hold.title: $K(o) = (t, x, f)$
sp.hold.meaning: The holding thread thread $t$, point $x$ and counter $f$ of a held end $o$.
sp.hold.why: One map records all data the measure reads.

args.name: t, x, f
args.meaning: holding thread thread, point and counter

sp.tk.title: $tk : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
sp.tk.meaning: $tk_t$ is the ticket count of thread $t$.
sp.tk.why: The termination measure of lock-free adequacy sums the tickets of all threads with their reserves, and links lower that sum.

sp.exists.title: Chosen per level
sp.exists.meaning: $\exists A, \Phi, U$, the held ends for the relation and for fuel, and the result type of each thread, chosen at each level.
sp.exists.why: O-New and F-New choose the session type of a new channel in separate existentials, so the protocols in $\Phi$ are not determined by $A$.

args.name: A
args.meaning: the held ends for the relation, $o \mapsto S@x$

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends for fuel, $o \mapsto S^{f}$

args.name: U
args.meaning: the result type of each thread

sp.tfree.title: $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$
sp.tfree.meaning: The result type holds no end.
sp.tfree.why: A main thread returning an end would leave that end's partner waiting.

sp.rel.title: Every thread live
sp.rel.meaning: $\forall t.\ q(t) \in E[\kappa_L]^W_n\llbracket K_t(A) \vdash U_t\rrbracket^{\varnothing}$, where $K_t(A)$ restricts $A$ to the ends held by $t$.
sp.rel.why: The per-thread relation at $\kappa_L$ excludes internal divergence and infinite chains of spawns.
sp.rel.signature: \forall t, e.\ q(t) = e \Rightarrow e \in E[\kappa_L]^{W}_{n}\llbracket K_t(A) \vdash U_t \rrbracket^{\varnothing}

args.name: K_t(A)
args.meaning: $A$ restricted to the ends held by $t$

sp.ty.title: $U_t \in \{T, \ast\}$
sp.ty.meaning: Each thread returns at $T$ or at $\ast$.
sp.ty.why: A thread that returns has a value in $V$ at $U_t$, and for $U_t \in \{T, \ast\}$ with $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$ that value holds no end, which the termination argument uses.
sp.ty.breaks: Without it, a finished thread could still hold an end.

sp.fuel.title: Each thread has fuel
sp.fuel.meaning: $\forall t.\ q(t) \in F^N_n\llbracket\Phi|_t ; tk_t \vdash \mathsf{thread}\ !\ (\infty, 0)\rrbracket$, where $\Phi|_t$ is $\Phi$ on the ends that $K$ gives to $t$.
sp.fuel.why: The counters of $\Phi$ are those recorded in $K$, so they are the same at every level.

args.name: \Phi|_t
args.meaning: $\Phi$ on the ends that $K$ gives to $t$

sp.pts.title: Points and counters from $K$
sp.pts.meaning: $K(o) = (t, x, f)$ implies that $o$ is at $x$ in $A$ and has counter $f$ in $\Phi$.
sp.pts.why: Points and counters are fixed outside the step index.

sp.dom.title: $\mathrm{dom}\,A = \mathrm{dom}\,\Phi = \mathrm{dom}\,K$
sp.dom.meaning: $A$, $\Phi$ and $K$ describe the same held ends.
sp.dom.why: Lock-free adequacy reads the protocol of an end of $K$, and of its dual end, to decide idleness, and a synchronization updates $\Phi$ and $K$ together.
sp.dom.breaks: Without it, a held end could lack a protocol, and idleness of a waiting end would be undefined.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, a finite map $o \mapsto S^{f}$ from ends to a protocol and a counter $f \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

args.name: K
args.meaning: the ownership map of the annotated configuration

sp.owner.title: Holding threads exist
sp.owner.why: A thread waiting on an end needs its partner's holding thread to be a thread of $q$, so the dependency of waiting threads is a relation on threads.
sp.owner.breaks: Without it, an end could be held by a thread that no longer exists, and its partner would wait forever.

args.name: o, t
args.meaning: a held end and the thread holding it

sp.closed.title: Held ends restricted or interface
sp.closed.why: For $\Sigma = \varnothing$ each held end is restricted, so the lock-free process relation holds both ends of each channel it acts on. Composition splits held ends along this condition.
sp.closed.breaks: Without it, a closed process could hold an end whose partner nobody holds, and the thread holding it would wait forever.

sp.pair.title: Restricted partners held
sp.pair.why: The partner of an internal end is held by some thread.
sp.pair.example: Both ends of $c$ in the pair of closes.

sp.sdual.title: Restricted pairs dual
sp.sdual.why: Internal partners are at dual points with dual session types.
sp.sdual.signature: A(o) = S@x \land A(\overline{o}) = S'@x' \land \mathsf{ech}\,o \in C \Rightarrow x' = \overline{x} \land \mathsf{sdual}\,S\,S'

args.name: o
args.meaning: an end of a restricted channel

sp.pdual.title: Restricted protocols dual
sp.pdual.why: Lock-free adequacy reads idleness from $\Phi$, and duality transfers idleness from an end to its dual end.

args.name: P, P'
args.meaning: the protocols of the two ends

sp.sig.title: Interface entries in $A$
sp.sig.why: Restricting a cut makes its channels internal, and their dual entries in $A$ come from $\Sigma$ through this condition.
sp.sig.breaks: Without it, a channel restricted at composition could have non-dual entries in $A$.

sp.psig.title: Interface protocols in $\Phi$
sp.psig.meaning: $\Sigma(o) = S@x$ implies $\Phi(o) = S^{f}$ for some counter $f$.
sp.psig.why: At composition the protocols of the cut come from $\Sigma$, which typing makes dual.

sp.fin.title: Finite counters
sp.fin.why: The termination measure reads every counter as a natural number.

sp.lfsem.title: $\Sigma \Vvdash_W p : T$
sp.lfsem.meaning: $\exists N \in \mathbb{N}, a, \chi.\ \mathsf{erase}(q_a) = p \land \forall n.\ a \in S^{N,W,\chi}_n\llbracket\Sigma \vdash T\rrbracket$.
sp.lfsem.why: The lock-free process relation alone suffices, and absence of internal divergence of the lock-free process relation gives what a process conjunct would.
sp.lfsem.example: The lock-free fundamental theorem concludes this judgment.

args.name: N, a
args.meaning: the counter bound and the annotated configuration, fixed before $n$

sp.exists-before-forall.title: $\exists$ before $\forall n$
sp.exists-before-forall.meaning: $N$, the state $a$ and the creation choice $\chi$ are fixed before the level quantifier.
sp.exists-before-forall.why: Ownership, points, counters and the placement of new channels are then the same at every level.
sp.exists-before-forall.breaks: A placement chosen per level lets the main thread wait forever in every fair run.

sp.chi.title: Creation choice $\chi$
sp.chi.meaning: A thread creates a channel from the term $e$ while it holds $\Theta$. For the fresh root $a$, $\chi(e, \Theta)(a) = (\pi, C)$ gives the position $\pi$, either $a$ or a field $x\cdot\kappa$, and the facts $C$ over $a$ and the points of $\Theta$.
sp.chi.why: The lock-free process relation fixes its annotated configuration before the level, and after a creation it records the point of the new ends. The judgment fixes $\chi$ before the level too, so the point and the facts of each creation are the same at every level. For a typed thread $\chi$ is the choice of its E-New step.
sp.chi.breaks: With the choice inside O-New, each level picks its own $\pi$ and $C$, and the recorded point matches no single choice.
sp.chi.example: $\chi(e, \Theta)(a) = (a\cdot 0, \{\rho \prec \overline{a\cdot 0}\})$ for the second creation of the cycle example.

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 2.

O-New.chi.title: $(\pi, C) = \chi(e, \Theta)(a)$
O-New.chi.meaning: Under lock freedom the position and the facts of the creation are those of the creation choice $\chi$.
O-New.chi.why: The choice is then the same at every level.
O-New.chi.example: Under deadlock freedom O-New picks $\pi$ and $C$ at each level.

args.name: \pi
args.meaning: the position of the new channel

deviations.reason: Not yet in the Rocq, see .claude/notes/redesign/pending.md, entry 2.

sp.next.title: $\mathsf{lf\_next}^{\chi}$
sp.next.why: A creation places the new ends at the position $\chi$ chooses with counter $N$ and grows the world by the facts $\chi$ chooses. An action moves its end to the next point and resets its counter to $N$. A transfer moves the ends to the receiving thread and decrements their counters. A link uses a ticket and renames, and a spawn splits the tickets. None of these depends on the level.
sp.next.example: One step of the lock-free process relation along an event.

sp.own.title: $\mathsf{consistent}(a, A, \Phi)$
sp.own.meaning: The ownership map $K$ of the annotated configuration agrees with $A$ and $\Phi$. Each held end is held by one thread of the configuration and is internal or in the interface. Both ends of an internal channel are held, at dual types, points and protocols. Interface entries come from $\Sigma$, and counters are finite.
sp.own.why: Lock-free adequacy reads the thread holding an end, its point and its counter from $K$, and concludes that the dual end of an internal end is held by some thread at the dual protocol.
sp.own.breaks: Without it a thread could wait on an end whose dual end no thread holds, and the chain of waits in the proof of adequacy would break off.
sp.own.example: Two threads closing $c^{+}$ and $c^{-}$, each holding one end, with $C = \{c\}$.

args.name: A
args.meaning: the held ends for the relation

sr.FE.title: Fuel $F^N_n\llbracket\Phi ; tk \vdash \sigma\ !\ (d, r)\rrbracket$
sr.FE.meaning: The thread holds the ends $\Phi$ and $tk$ tickets and has fuel for $n$ more steps to return at $\sigma$ within $d$ actions with $r$ tickets left, at counter bound $N$.
sr.FE.why: It bounds postponement and links per thread, independent of points. It is indexed by $n$, as $E$ is, so it is written as membership and not as a judgment.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, a finite map $o \mapsto S^{f}$ from ends to a protocol and a counter $f \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

args.name: \sigma
args.meaning: the result, a credited type or $\mathsf{thread}$

args.name: d
args.meaning: the frame, the actions left before returning, $d \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

args.name: r
args.meaning: the reserve, the tickets kept on return, $r \in \mathbb{N}$

sr.FV.title: Values with fuel, $FV^N_n\llbracket\Phi \vdash \sigma\rrbracket$
sr.FV.meaning: The value holds exactly the ends $\Phi$, and their counters meet the credits of $\sigma$.
sr.FV.why: Values have the protocols and counters of their ends.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, a finite map $o \mapsto S^{f}$ from ends to a protocol and a counter $f \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

sr.act.title: $\mathsf{act}\,o$
sr.act.meaning: The common premise of every action on $o$, F-Wait and F-Count.
sr.act.why: Send, receive, close, select and branch share this premise.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, a finite map $o \mapsto S^{f}$ from ends to a protocol and a counter $f \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$

sr.vthunk.title: $\mathsf{Vthunk}^W_n(\Theta)$
sr.vthunk.meaning: The predicate of a spawned thunk owning $\Theta$.
sr.vthunk.why: A spawned thunk needs neither lower nor upper point.

sr.thunk.title: $\mathsf{thunk}(e)$
sr.thunk.why: Forcing $!e$ steps to $e[!e]$, which the thunk delays by one $\lambda$.

sr.size.title: $\mathsf{size}\,T$
sr.size.meaning: The size of a type, with a box counting $3 + \mathsf{size}\,U$.
sr.size.why: It makes $V$ at a box read $V$ at the smaller thunk type.

sr.irred.title: $\mathsf{irred}\,e$
sr.irred.meaning: $e$ takes no step, $\neg\exists \alpha, e'.\ e \xrightarrow{\alpha} e'$.
sr.irred.why: Values and stuck terms are irreducible.

sr.ready.title: $\mathsf{ready}_W(\Theta \mid F, t)$
sr.ready.meaning: Readiness of a term with environment $\Theta$ and future $F$ in world $W$.

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, a finite set of points

sr.readyp.title: $\mathsf{ready}_W(\Sigma, p)$
sr.readyp.meaning: Readiness of a process with interface $\Sigma$ in world $W$.
sr.readyp.why: It excludes circular waiting across the interface.

sr.obl.title: $\mathsf{Obl}_\alpha(e')$
sr.obl.meaning: The obligation of the step label $\alpha$, one of O-Beta to O-Link.
sr.obl.why: Each label has its own obligation, read off the label.

sr.pobl.title: $\mathsf{Pobl}_{ev}(p')$
sr.pobl.meaning: The obligation of the event $ev$, one of Q-Tau to Q-Link.
sr.pobl.why: Each event has its own obligation, read off the event.
sr.pobl.example: $\mathsf{Pobl}_{ev}$ is Q-Tau for an internal event.

sr.fobl.title: $\mathsf{Fobl}^N_\alpha(e')$
sr.fobl.meaning: The fuel obligation of the step label $\alpha$, one of F-Beta to F-Link.
sr.fobl.why: Each label has its own fuel update.

sr.fuseok.title: $(h, D) \in \mathsf{Fus}(\Sigma, p)$
sr.fuseok.meaning: $(h, D)$ is an admissible fusion of the held ends of $p$ with interface $\Sigma$.
sr.fuseok.why: One notion covers renaming, internalizing pairs and the renaming of a link.

args.name: D
args.meaning: the channels restricted by the fusion

sr.sdrop.title: $(h, D)\cdot\Sigma$
sr.sdrop.meaning: $\Sigma$ renamed by $h$, without the ends of the channels $D$, in the Rocq $\mathsf{sdrop}\,D\,(h\,\Sigma)$.
sr.sdrop.why: The channels of $D$ become restricted and leave the interface.

sr.pfuse.title: $(h, D)\cdot p$
sr.pfuse.meaning: $p$ renamed by $h$ with the channels $D$ added to the restricted set, in the Rocq $\mathsf{pfuse}\,h\,D\,p$.
sr.pfuse.why: It is the process after the fusion.

sr.pirred.title: $\mathsf{pirred}\,p$
sr.pirred.why: P-Stop applies exactly to irreducible processes.

sr.held.title: Held ends
sr.held.why: A process holds its interface ends and both ends of every restricted channel.

sr.gch.title: $\mathsf{gch}_h$
sr.gch.why: Restricted sets are sets of channels, so $h$ acts on them through its action on $c^{+}$.

sr.tenv-erase.title: $|\Delta|$
sr.tenv-erase.meaning: The ends of $\Delta$ with their session types and points, each entry $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ becoming $S@x$.
sr.tenv-erase.why: \inmode{lf}{$E$ reads ends only, and no credit.}

sr.fvagg.title: Products, sums and existentials in $FV$
sr.fvagg.meaning: $\otimes$ splits $\Phi$ disjointly between its parts, $\oplus$ checks the injected part, and $\exists$ checks its body.
sr.fvagg.why: Only ends and closures have credits, so these types only pass $\Phi$ on.

args.name: \Phi
args.meaning: the held ends, split among the parts

th.adequacy.title: Adequacy
th.adequacy.meaning: For strict $W$, if $\varnothing \vDash_W p : T$ then $p$ is deadlock free.
th.adequacy.why: It turns the semantic judgment into the safety property. In a world with a cycle in $\prec_W$ readiness holds vacuously for threads waiting round the cycle, so strictness is needed.
th.adequacy.breaks: Without $\mathsf{strict}\,W$ the premise holds for a cyclic world in which two threads wait on each other.
th.adequacy.example: Two threads closing the two ends of $c$ are deadlock free.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.lf-adequacy.title: Lock-free adequacy
th.lf-adequacy.meaning: For $W$ with $\mathsf{strict}\,W$ and $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$, if $\varnothing \Vvdash_W p : T$ then $p$ is lock free.
th.lf-adequacy.why: A pending thread waits for the thread holding the partner of its end. The proof follows this chain of waiting threads and shows it is finite, by a measure of the point of the awaited end, the tickets left and the counter, which decreases because $\prec_W$ is well-founded.
th.lf-adequacy.breaks: Without $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$ an infinite descending chain of points lets a thread wait forever along an infinite chain of holding threads.
th.lf-adequacy.example: Two threads closing the two ends of $c$ are lock free.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.lf-thread-progress.title: Thread progress
th.lf-thread-progress.meaning: Under the premises of lock-free adequacy, every run $(r, l)$ with $\mathsf{erase}(r\,0) = p$, $\mathsf{maximal}\,(r, l)$ and $\mathsf{wfair}\,(r, l)$ satisfies $\mathsf{thread\_progress\_run}\,(r, l)$.
th.lf-thread-progress.why: Every thread eventually returns a value or takes part in a session step, so no thread, pending or not, is postponed forever.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: (r, l)
args.meaning: a run, $r\,i$ the configuration and $l\,i$ the event at position $i$

th.fundamental.title: Fundamental theorem
th.fundamental.meaning: For strict $W$, $\varnothing ; \Delta \vdash^{F}_{W} t : T$ implies $\Delta \vDash^{F}_{W} t : T$.
th.fundamental.why: Each typing rule has a semantic counterpart that holds at every level, and the theorem is the induction on the derivation.
th.fundamental.example: The main thread of the cycle example satisfies the semantic judgment.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context of ends and variables

th.fundamental-typed.title: Fundamental theorem for annotated typing
th.fundamental-typed.meaning: For strict $W$ and every $N$, the annotated typing judgment implies the semantic judgment at $\Delta_{df}$ and $T_{df}$.
th.fundamental-typed.why: Erasing the annotations of an annotated derivation gives a deadlock-free derivation, to which the fundamental theorem applies.
th.fundamental-typed.example: The client and server main at $N = \infty$.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context of ends and variables

th.live-fundamental.title: Live fundamental theorem
th.live-fundamental.meaning: For strict $W$, $\varnothing ; \Delta \vdash^{F}_{W} t : T$ and $\varnothing \vdash\!\triangleright t$ imply $\Delta \mathrel{|\!\!\vDash}^{F}_{W} t : T$.
th.live-fundamental.why: The guard lets a box recurse only after an action, so every recursive call is read at a lower level, as the least fixpoint of the relation at $kappa_L$ requires.
th.live-fundamental.breaks: Without the guard the statement is false, $!(f = \mathsf{force}\,f)$ types and satisfies no live judgment.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context of ends and variables

th.live-fundamental-typed.title: Live fundamental theorem for annotated typing
th.live-fundamental-typed.meaning: For strict $W$, the annotated typing judgment with $\varnothing \vdash\!\triangleright t$ implies the live judgment at erased environments and type.
th.live-fundamental-typed.why: Lock-free soundness obtains the relation at $kappa_L$ of each thread from this theorem.
th.live-fundamental-typed.example: A thread typed by P-Term at finite $N$.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

th.fundamental-proc.title: Fundamental theorem for processes
th.fundamental-proc.meaning: $\Sigma \vdash\inmode{lf}{^{\infty}}_{W} p : T$ implies $\Sigma \vDash_W p : T$. P-Term asks a strict world, and P-Connect keeps the join strict, so the derivation gives $\mathsf{strict}\,W$ and the theorem has no such premise.
th.fundamental-proc.why: It is an induction on the process derivation with the semantic P-Term and P-Connect as cases.
th.fundamental-proc.example: Two threads closing the two ends of $c$.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.lf-fundamental.title: Lock-free fundamental theorem
th.lf-fundamental.why: The fuel of each thread comes from its cost typing at finite $N$ with the ticket premise of P-Term, and its relation at $kappa_L$ from its guarded typing.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: N
args.meaning: the counter bound, a natural number for lock freedom

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.sem-p-term.title: Semantic P-Term
th.sem-p-term.meaning: If $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$, $\mathsf{sth}\,\Theta\,\Sigma\,\Theta_B\,C$ and $t \in E[\kappa]^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Theta \vdash T\rrbracket^{\varnothing}$, then $(C, \{t\}) \in P[\kappa]^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Sigma \vdash T\rrbracket$.
th.sem-p-term.why: It is P-Term in the relation. When $t$ spawns $v$, the child receives exactly the ends $\mathsf{fends}(v)$, which $V$ fixes by $\mathrm{dom}\,\Theta = \mathsf{fends}(v)$, and the proof composes parent and child as P-Connect does.

args.name: \kappa
args.meaning: a cost table, $\kappa_{DF}$ for deadlock freedom and $\kappa_L$ for liveness

args.name: \Theta_B
args.meaning: the entries of the restricted ends

th.sth.title: $\mathsf{sth}\,\Theta\,\Sigma\,\Theta_B\,C$
th.sth.meaning: $\Theta = \Sigma \cup \Theta_B$, $\mathrm{dom}\,\Theta_B = \mathsf{ends}(C)$, $\mathsf{chans}\,\Sigma \cap C = \varnothing$, $\mathsf{pfree}\,\Sigma$, and for every $c \in C$ the two entries of $\Theta_B$ are dual at dual points.
th.sth.why: These are the environment premises of P-Term, as the semantic proof uses these premises.

args.name: \Theta
args.meaning: the ends held by the term

args.name: \Theta_B
args.meaning: the entries of the ends of restricted channels

th.sem-p-connect.title: Semantic P-Connect
th.sem-p-connect.meaning: If $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$, $\mathsf{conn}$, $p_1 \in P^{W_1}_n\llbracket\Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_C \vdash T\rrbracket$ and $p_2 \in P^{W_2}_n\llbracket\Sigma_2 \cup \Sigma_D \vdash \ast\rrbracket$, then $p_1 \parallel_{\Sigma_C} p_2 \in P^{W_1 \sqcup W_2}_n\llbracket\Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_2 \vdash T\rrbracket$.
th.sem-p-connect.why: It is P-Connect in the relation, for every level $n$ and every cost table.
th.sem-p-connect.example: Two threads closing $c^{+}$ and $c^{-}$, cut at $c$.
th.sem-p-connect.signature: \mathsf{tfree}\,T \land \mathsf{conn} \land p_1 \in P^{W_1}_{n}\llbracket\Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_C \vdash T\rrbracket \land p_2 \in P^{W_2}_{n}\llbracket\Sigma_2 \cup \Sigma_D \vdash \ast\rrbracket \Rightarrow p_1 \parallel_{\Sigma_C} p_2 \in P^{W_1 \sqcup W_2}_{n}\llbracket\Sigma_1 \cup \Sigma_2 \vdash T\rrbracket

th.lf-p-term.title: P-Term in the lock-free process relation
th.lf-p-term.meaning: For strict $W$, a thread with $\Sigma \Vdash^{N}_{W} (C_0, \{t\}) : T$ derived by P-Term satisfies $\Sigma \Vvdash_W (C_0, \{t\}) : T$.
th.lf-p-term.why: It is P-Term read in the lock-free process relation.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

th.Erel-bind.title: Bind
th.Erel-bind.meaning: For every cost table, if $e \in E^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Theta_1 \vdash T\rrbracket^{F \cup \mathsf{ap}\,\Theta_2}$ and $f[v] \in E^{W'}_{j}\llbracket\Theta_v \cup \Theta_2 \vdash U\rrbracket^{F}$ for all $W' \sqsupseteq W$, $j \leq n$ and $v \in V^{W'}_{j}\llbracket\Theta_v \vdash T\rrbracket$, then $f[e] \in E^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Theta_1 \cup \Theta_2 \vdash U\rrbracket^{F}$.
th.Erel-bind.why: Every rule with a subterm runs the subterm first. The frame holds $\Theta_2$ while the hole runs, so the hole must not wait above $\mathsf{ap}\,\Theta_2$.
th.Erel-bind.signature: e \in E^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Theta_1 \vdash T\rrbracket^{F \cup \mathsf{ap}\,\Theta_2} \land (\forall W' \sqsupseteq W, j \leq n, v.\ \ldots) \Rightarrow f[e] \in E^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Theta_1 \cup \Theta_2 \vdash U\rrbracket^{F}

args.name: \Theta_2
args.meaning: the ends the frame holds while $e$ runs

args.name: W', j, v
args.meaning: every later world, every level $j \leq n$ and every value $v$ in $V^{W'}_{j}$ that $e$ may return

th.soundness.title: Soundness
th.soundness.meaning: $\varnothing \vdash\inmode{lf}{^{\infty}}_{W} p : T$ implies that $p$ is deadlock free.
th.soundness.why: The fundamental theorem for processes followed by adequacy.
th.soundness.example: The cycle example is deadlock free.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.soundness-source.title: Soundness for source terms
th.soundness-source.meaning: For strict $W$, $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$ and $\varnothing ; \varnothing \vdash^{\varnothing}_{W} t : T$, the process $(\varnothing, \{t\})$ is deadlock free.
th.soundness-source.why: A source term creates channels only at fresh roots and at fields of held ends, so it is P-Term with $\Sigma = \varnothing$ and $C_0 = \varnothing$.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: t
args.meaning: a source term, the main thread

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.lf-soundness.title: Lock-free soundness
th.lf-soundness.meaning: For $W$ with $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$, $\varnothing \Vdash^{N}_{W} p : T$ implies that $p$ is lock free.
th.lf-soundness.why: The lock-free fundamental theorem followed by lock-free adequacy.
th.lf-soundness.example: The cycle example is lock free.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: N
args.meaning: the counter bound, a natural number for lock freedom

args.name: T
args.meaning: the result type of the main thread

th.lf-soundness-source.title: Lock-free soundness for source terms
th.lf-soundness-source.meaning: For $W$ with $\mathsf{strict}\,W$ and $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$, $N \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$, a typing $\varnothing ; \varnothing \vdash^{\varnothing}_{W\inmode{lf}{,N}} t : T\ !\ (c, \vartheta)$, $\vartheta(0) \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varnothing \vdash\!\triangleright t$, the process $(\varnothing, \{t\})$ is lock free.
th.lf-soundness-source.why: The premises are those of P-Term at finite $N$ with $\Sigma = \varnothing$ and $C_0 = \varnothing$, plus the guard. Lock-free soundness then applies.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

args.name: N
args.meaning: the counter bound, a natural number for lock freedom

th.conservative.title: Conservativity
th.conservative.meaning: The annotated typing judgment at $N = \infty$ derives some $T_{df}\ !\ \varepsilon$ iff the deadlock-free judgment derives $T_{df}$, at erased contexts.
th.conservative.why: Deadlock-free typing is the annotated typing judgment with credits, costs and ticket needs ignored, so one set of rules serves both.

args.name: a, c, \vartheta
args.meaning: some credit, cost and ticket need

th.typed-dftyped.title: Erasure to deadlock-free typing
th.typed-dftyped.meaning: For every $N$, erasing the annotations of an annotated derivation gives a deadlock-free derivation.
th.typed-dftyped.why: Hence every lock-free typing is also a deadlock-free typing.
th.typed-dftyped.example: The cycle at $N = 2$ erases to its deadlock-free typing.

th.wfworld.title: $\mathsf{wfworld}\,W$
th.wfworld.meaning: $\prec_W$ is well-founded, there is no infinite descending chain $x_0 \succ_W x_1 \succ_W \cdots$.
th.wfworld.why: A chain of waiting threads descends in $\prec_W$, so well-foundedness makes it finite. Deadlock freedom does not need well-foundedness.
th.wfworld.example: Every world of the lock-free examples is well-founded.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world, the order $\prec_W$ the semantic judgments read

th.cost-fundamental.title: Cost fundamental theorem
th.cost-fundamental.meaning: The annotated typing judgment implies the semantic cost judgment $\Delta \vDash^{N} e : T\ !\ \varepsilon$.
th.cost-fundamental.why: It is the cost half of the annotated typing judgment, proved rule by rule.

th.fsem-of-cost.title: Fuel from cost typing
th.fsem-of-cost.meaning: If $\varnothing ; \Delta \vdash^{\varnothing}_{W\inmode{lf}{,N}} e : T\ !\ (c, \vartheta)$, $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$, $\mathsf{cr}(\Delta) \leq N$ and $\vartheta(0) \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\mathsf{fsem}\,N\,(\mathsf{sty} \circ \Delta)\,e$.
th.fsem-of-cost.why: P-Term gives every end credit $N$, so the cost judgment yields the per-thread fuel that lock freedom needs.
th.fsem-of-cost.breaks: If a closure could mention an end it does not own, the forwarder could receive a closure that owns nothing and would have no fuel after spawning the closure.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the ends of the thread with their credits

th.crle.title: $\mathsf{cr}(\Delta) \leq N$
th.crle.meaning: Every credit in $\Delta$ is at most the counter bound $N$, that is $a \leq N$ for every entry $(S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ or $(T \multimap U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ of $\Delta$.
th.crle.why: A thread starts with every counter at $N$, so its credits may guarantee no more than $N$.
th.crle.breaks: A credit above $N$ would allow more postponement than a fresh counter allows.

ann.fin0.title: $\vartheta(0) \in \mathbb{N}$
ann.fin0.meaning: The ticket need of a whole thread, which keeps no reserve, is a finite number.
ann.fin0.why: Then some ticket count $tk \geq \vartheta(0)$ covers every link of the thread.
ann.fin0.breaks: A need that is $\infty$ at reserve $0$ belongs to a thread that may link without bound.

args.name: \vartheta
args.meaning: the ticket need of the thread

th.Prel.title: The process relation $P$
th.Prel.meaning: $P[\kappa]^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Sigma \vdash T\rrbracket$, the processes in the relation at table $\kappa$, world $W$, level $n$, interface $\Sigma$ and result $T$.
th.Prel.why: The semantic process judgment asks membership at every level $n$.
th.Prel.example: Two threads closing $c^{+}$ and $c^{-}$ lie in $P^{W}_{n}\llbracket\varnothing \vdash \ast\rrbracket$ for every $n$.

th.Erel.title: The term relation $E$
th.Erel.meaning: $E[\kappa]^{W}_{n}\llbracket\Theta \vdash T\rrbracket^{F}$ is the set of terms in the relation at cost table $\kappa$, world $W$ and level $n$, for ends $\Theta$, result $T$ and future $F$.
th.Erel.why: The semantic term judgment asks membership at each level and for each grounding of the variables.

th.Vrel.title: The value relation $V$
th.Vrel.meaning: $V^{W}_{j}\llbracket\Theta \vdash T\rrbracket$ is the set of values in the relation at world $W$ and level $j$, for ends $\Theta$ and type $T$.
th.Vrel.why: A term in $E$ that is irreducible is a value in $V$.

th.soup.title: The lock-free process relation $S^{N,W,chi}_{n}$
th.soup.meaning: $a \in S^{N,W,chi}_{n}\llbracket\Sigma \vdash T\rrbracket$ holds of an annotated configuration $a$ when every thread of $a$ is in the relation at $kappa_L$ and has fuel at index $n$, with the ownership, points and counters that $a$ records.
th.soup.why: The state $a$ is fixed outside the index, so ownership is the same at every index $n$.
th.soup.example: The state of two threads closing $c^{+}$ and $c^{-}$.

th.qa.title: $q_a$

th.qa.why: An annotated configuration is a configuration together with ownership and tickets.

th.conn.title: $\mathsf{conn}$
th.conn.meaning: The side conditions of P-Connect, with $\Sigma_D$ the partners of $\Sigma_C$ dual up to $\approx$ at dual points.
th.conn.why: They make the composite a process in which every channel belongs to one side.

th.par.title: $p_1 \parallel_{\Sigma_C} p_2$
th.par.meaning: The composite $(C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \mathsf{chans}\,\Sigma_C, E_1 \uplus E_2)$ of $p_1 = (C_1, E_1)$ and $p_2 = (C_2, E_2)$.
th.par.why: After composition the two sides communicate on the cut, which no outside process holds.

th.df.title: Erasure $X_{df}$
th.df.meaning: $\Delta_{df}$ and $T_{df}$ drop every credit, cost and ticket need and keep session types, points and facts.
th.df.why: Deadlock-free typing and the relations read no annotation.

th.styof.title: $\Delta\inmode{lf}{^{N}}$
th.styof.meaning: The held ends of $\Delta$ for fuel, each at counter $N$. An entry $o \mapsto (S@x)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ of $\Delta$ becomes $o \mapsto S\inmode{lf}{^{N}}$.
th.styof.why: Fuel reads protocols and counters and ignores points and credits. A thread starts with each counter at $N$.

args.name: \Delta

th.tpr.title: $\mathsf{thread\_progress\_run}$
th.tpr.meaning: For a run $(r, l)$, $\mathsf{thread\_progress\_run}\,(r, l)$ holds iff each thread $t$ of each position $i$ later stops or acts. That is, some $j \geq i$ exists at which $t$ is a value in $r\,j$ or takes part in the step $l\,j$ by a session action.
th.tpr.why: It states lock freedom per run for each thread, including the threads that are not pending. A thread that is neither stopped nor acting forever would be postponed without end.
th.tpr.example: In a run of two threads closing $c^{+}$ and $c^{-}$, both threads take part in the close step.

args.name: (r, l)
args.meaning: a run, $r\,i$ the configuration and $l\,i$ the event at position $i$

examples.title: Client and server cycle
examples.lead: Two loops that call themselves forever over the same two channels are deadlock free, because one constraint orders the points of all their rounds at once.
examples.meaning: A client sends on $a$ and then receives on $b$, and a server receives on $a$ and then sends on $b$, both forever. The second $\mathsf{new}$ places $b$ at the field $\rho\cdot 0$ of the root of $a$ and states the facts $C$ at $(\rho, \rho\cdot 0, \rho\cdot 1)$. Each recursive call is at the next points $(\iota^{+}, \kappa^{+}, \zeta)$, where $C$ states the same facts again.

examples.title: Cycle
examples.lead: Two threads that use two channels in the same order type, because creating the second channel states the two order facts the threads need.
examples.code:
cycle = let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in          -- c at ρ
        let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in          -- d at ρ·0, C = {ρ ≺ (ρ·0)‾, ρ‾ ≺ ρ·0}
        let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = u in let ∗ = close c′ in close d′) in
        let ∗ = close c in close d
examples.meaning: Main closes $c$ and then $d$, and the spawned thread closes $c'$ and then $d'$. Each thread waits on one channel while it holds an end of the other. The second $\mathsf{new}$ states exactly the two facts this requires, $\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}$ for main and $\overline{\rho} \prec \rho\cdot 0$ for the spawned thread.

examples.title: A channel between two box arguments
examples.lead: A procedure can create a channel whose point lies between the points of two channels it receives as arguments.
examples.code:
between : □(∀ι κ. C. ∗ ⊸ Close@ι ⊗ Close@κ ⊸^κ ∗)
between = !(f = λp. let ⟨c, e⟩ = p in
                    let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in        -- d at ι·0
                    let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = u in close d′) in
                    let ∗ = close c in let ∗ = close d in close e)
-- C = {ι ≺ κ, ι ≺ κ‾, ι ≺ δ‾, δ ≺ κ, δ ≺ κ‾},  δ = ι·0
main: c by new at ρ, e by new at ρ·1, force between at (ρ, ρ·1)
examples.meaning: The box creates a channel $d$ while it holds two arguments $c$ and $e$, and closes $c$, $d$ and $e$ in this order. E-New places $d$ at the field $\iota\cdot 0$ of the point of $c$. The facts of the box constraint then order $d$ between $c$ and $e$, and no point between two box points is needed.

examples.title: A channel that acts several times
examples.lead: A new channel can act several times while an older end is held, because a box constraint may state infinitely many facts.
examples.code:
many = !(f = λp. let ⟨c, e⟩ = p in
                 let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in         -- d at δ
                 let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = u in
                                     let ⟨v, d′⟩ = recv d′ in let ∗ = v in
                                     let ⟨w, d′⟩ = recv d′ in let ∗ = w in close d′) in
                 let ∗ = close c in
                 let ∗ = close (send ⟨∗, send ⟨∗, d⟩⟩) in close e)
-- C = {ι ≺ κ, ι ≺ κ‾, ι ≺ δ‾} ∪ {δ+k ≺ κ, δ+k ≺ κ‾ | k},  δ = ι·0
examples.meaning: The new end $d$ sends twice and closes while the box holds $e$. The constraint of the box is infinite, one pair of facts for each offset of $\delta$, so $d$ may act at $\delta$, $\delta^{+}$ and $\delta^{++}$ below the point $\kappa$ of $e$.

examples.title: The factory
examples.lead: One way of creating a channel admits two typings, at a fresh root hidden in an existential or at a field of an end the creator holds.
examples.code:
mk₀  = !(f = λu. let ∗ = u in let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in
                let ∗ = spawn (λv. let ∗ = v in close (send ⟨∗, c⟩)) in c′)
mk₁  = !(f = λp. let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in
                let ∗ = spawn (λv. let ∗ = v in close (send ⟨∗, c⟩)) in ⟨p, c′⟩)
main = let p = (force mk₀) ∗ in let ⟨p, q⟩ = (force mk₁) p in
       let ∗ = recvclose p in recvclose q
-- mk₀ places c at a fresh ρ with C(ρ) = {ρ‾ ≺ ρ·0, ρ‾⁺ ≺ ρ·0}, mk₁ at ι·0 for p at ι
-- mk₀ : □(∗ ⊸ ∃^⊥ ι. C(ι). (?∗.Close)@ι‾)
examples.meaning: Each box creates a channel, spawns a sender on one end and returns the other end. $\mathsf{mk}_0$ places the channel at a fresh root and returns it packed in an existential. $\mathsf{mk}_1$ places it at a field of the end it receives. The two boxes type one creation in the two ways E-New allows.

examples.title: The growing ring
examples.lead: A ring of threads that grows forever is lock free.
examples.code:
Sch  = µα. ?(κ. α@κ).Close
ring : □(∀ι₁ ι₂. Cr. ∗ ⊸ (Sch@ι₁ ⊗ S̄ch@ι₂ ⊸^{ι₁+1} ∗))
ring = !(f = λp. let ⟨x, y⟩ = p in
           let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in                -- a at ι₂·0
           let ∗ = spawn (λw. let ∗ = w in close (send ⟨a, y⟩)) in
           let ⟨b, b′⟩ = new in                -- b at ι₁·1
           let ⟨z, x⟩ = recv x in let ∗ = close x in
           let ∗ = spawn (λw. let ∗ = w in (force f) ⟨z, b′⟩) in
           spawn (λw. let ∗ = w in (force f) ⟨b, a′⟩))
main = let ⟨e, e′⟩ = new in (force ring) ⟨e, e′⟩
examples.meaning: Each round of the ring receives an end $z$ on $x$, spawns two copies of itself, and so the ring grows forever. E-New places $b$ at $\iota_1\cdot 1$ while $x$ is held at $\iota_1$, before the receive on $x$. The ring is lock free, with lock-free typing at $N = 4$.

examples.title: Two threads closing one channel
examples.lead: The smallest process built from two typed threads by the process rules.
examples.code:
cl c⁺ ∥ cl c⁻,   cl o = close o
-- each thread by P-Term at every finite N over its end, cut c by P-Connect at exactly dual types
examples.meaning: Two threads each close one end of $c$. P-Term types each thread over its end, and P-Connect cuts $c$ at dual types in a world without facts. It is the smallest use of the two process rules.

examples.title: Guard rejections
examples.lead: Recursion that can run forever without a session action is outside lock-free typing.
examples.code:
div_box     = !(f = force f)                         -- loops on β steps
pn_fix      = !(f = λx. (force f) x)                  -- fix λx.x
cx_box      = !(f = let ∗ = (force f) ∗ in λy. y)     -- recurses before returning
spawn_loop  = !(f = λc. spawn (λ_. (force f) c))      -- spawns forever
examples.meaning: Each box uses its own variable before its first session action. The first loops on $\beta$ steps, the second is $\mathsf{fix}\,\lambda x.\,x$, the third recurses before it returns, and the fourth spawns forever. The guard rejects all four, so they are outside lock-free typing.

examples.title: Guard acceptances
examples.lead: Recursion that performs a session action before each recursive call passes the guard.
examples.code:
loop  = !(f = λx. let ⟨v, x′⟩ = recv x in (force f) x′)
stage = !(f = λin. let ⟨v, in⟩ = recv in in let ∗ = close in in
                  let ⟨a, b⟩ = new in let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force f) b) in
                  close (send ⟨v, a⟩))                  -- a pipeline stage
examples.meaning: In both boxes a $\mathsf{recv}$ comes before the recursive call. A receive is a session action, so the guard checks the rest of the body under $\varnothing$, where the variable of the box is usable again.

examples.title: The spawn forwarder
examples.lead: A thread that receives closures and spawns them is lock free, because a received closure owns the ends it mentions.
examples.code:
fw o = let ⟨w, c⟩ = recv o in let ∗ = close c in spawn w
o : ?((∗ ⊸ ∗)^2).Close
dead_thunk q = λ_. let ∗ = Ω in close q
examples.meaning: The forwarder receives a closure on $o$ and spawns the closure as a new thread. $\mathsf{dead\_thunk}\,q$ mentions the end $q$ without owning it, so it is not a value in $FV$ and cannot arrive on $o$. Each closure the forwarder receives therefore owns its ends, and $\mathsf{fw}$ has fuel at each counter bound.

examples.title: The controller
examples.lead: An end that no thread ever acts on may be held across a loop of unbounded length.
examples.code:
main = let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in let ⟨b, b′⟩ = new in   -- a at ρ, b at ρ·0
       let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in                              -- c at ρ·2
       let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = u in (force srv) ⟨⟨a′, b′⟩, c′⟩) in
       (force cli) ⟨⟨a, b⟩, c⟩
cli  = !(f = λp. let ⟨q, k⟩ = p in let ⟨a, b⟩ = q in
                let a = send ⟨∗, a⟩ in let ⟨u, b⟩ = recv b in
                let ∗ = u in (force f) ⟨⟨a, b⟩, k⟩)
-- c sits at Skip on each side, an idle end
examples.meaning: The client sends on $a$ and receives on $b$ in each round, and holds the end $k$ at $\mathsf{Skip}@\chi$ throughout. Aging requires $c \leq a$ only of ends that are not idle. The idle end $k$ therefore has credit $0$ across rounds of unbounded cost.

examples.title: Self-computed flag
examples.lead: A thread that branches on a flag it computes itself is deadlock free, and only semantic typing shows it, because static typing checks the arm that never runs.
examples.code:
not     = λz. case z of inl w ⇒ inj₂ w | inr w ⇒ inj₁ w
thread  = case not (inj₂ ∗) of
            inl _ ⇒ let ∗ = close c in close d      -- runs
          | inr _ ⇒ let ∗ = close d in close c      -- never runs
partner = let ∗ = close c̄ in close d̄
-- the process ({c, d}, {thread, partner}), c at x, d at y
examples.meaning: The flag is always $\mathsf{inj}_1\,\ast$, so the thread closes $c$ before $d$. E-Case types both arms in one world. The first arm asks $x \prec \overline{y}$, the second asks $y \prec \overline{x}$, and the partner asks $\overline{x} \prec y$. The joint world has the cycle $y \prec \overline{x} \prec y$, and P-Connect asks a strict world. The relation reads only the steps the thread takes. After three $\beta$ steps the thread is in the first arm, which the fundamental theorem places in $E$ in a world with $x \prec \overline{y}$ alone. Semantic P-Connect joins it with the partner, the joint world has no cycle, and adequacy gives deadlock freedom. The rejection holds whatever points $c$ and $d$ get, and the map records it as an argument, with no Rocq proof.

examples.title: Two threads on one received flag
examples.lead: Two threads that branch on one flag sent by a third thread are deadlock free. A proof that follows the reductions of the whole process shows it, and a proof that puts each thread into the relation on its own fails.
examples.code:
A = case z of inl _ ⇒ let ∗ = close a in close b
             | inr _ ⇒ let ∗ = close b in close a
B = case z of inl _ ⇒ let ∗ = close ā in close b̄
             | inr _ ⇒ let ∗ = close b̄ in close ā
-- a at x, b at y, both threads receive the same flag z
examples.meaning: Both threads get the same flag, so they close $a$ and $b$ in the same order in every run. A received flag is any value of $V$ at $\ast \oplus \ast$, so each thread has to be in $E$ for both flags. With $\mathsf{inl}$ thread A closes $a$ while it holds $b$ and asks $x \prec \overline{y}$. With $\mathsf{inr}$ thread B closes $\overline{b}$ while it holds $\overline{a}$ and asks $\overline{y} \prec x$. The join of the two worlds then has a cycle, and P-Connect asks a strict join. One such thread alone fits in a strict world, the pair does not. The flag travels on an internal channel, so the process relation of the closed process reads only its actual reductions, in which both threads take the same branch. Following them puts the process in $P$ directly.

sem.part: the whole process, by its reductions
sem.rocq: argued, no Rocq proof. Thread by thread it fails: fp_unrealizable

examples.title: Postponement, a holding thread that never serves
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which one thread waits forever, because the thread holding its dual end never acts on that end.
examples.code:
chat = !(f = λa. let a = send ⟨∗, a⟩ in (force f) a)
loop = !(f = λ⟨a, b⟩. let ⟨u, a⟩ = recv a in let ∗ = u in (force f) ⟨a, b⟩)
main = let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in let ⟨b, b′⟩ = new in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force chat) a′) in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close b′) in
       (force loop) ⟨a, b⟩            -- holds b forever, close b′ waits forever
examples.meaning: Main holds $b$ while it runs a loop that never returns, and the thread with $b'$ waits forever while other threads step. Aging requires $c \leq a$ of each held end that is not idle. The loop has cost $\infty$, and $b$ has a finite credit, so the program has no lock-free typing.

deviations.reason: To be mechanized.

examples.title: Endless delegation, an end that travels forever
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which an end is sent back and forth forever while its partner waits.
examples.code:
pass = !(f = λ⟨e, x, y⟩. let x = send ⟨e, x⟩ in let ⟨e, y⟩ = recv y in (force f) ⟨e, x, y⟩)
back = !(f = λ⟨x, y⟩. let ⟨e, x⟩ = recv x in let y = send ⟨e, y⟩ in (force f) ⟨x, y⟩)
main = let ⟨e, e′⟩ = new in let ⟨x, x′⟩ = new in let ⟨y, y′⟩ = new in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close e′) in       -- waits for e forever
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force back) ⟨x′, y′⟩) in
       (force pass) ⟨e, x, y⟩                -- e goes back and forth forever
examples.meaning: Two threads send the end $e$ back and forth forever, and the thread with $e'$ waits. Each send passes $e$ on with its counter one lower. After finitely many sends no credit remains to send $e$ again, so the program has no lock-free typing.

deviations.reason: To be mechanized.

examples.title: Link refresh, a waiting thread that always faces a fresh end
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which links keep replacing the end a thread waits on.
examples.code:
refresh = !(f = λ⟨w, k⟩. let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in
                     let ∗ = link ⟨w, c⟩ in          -- the waiting thread now talks to c′
                     let k = send ⟨∗, k⟩ in           -- one step on another channel
                     (force f) ⟨c′, k⟩)
sink    = !(f = λk. let ⟨u, k⟩ = recv k in let ∗ = u in (force f) k)
main = let ⟨w, w′⟩ = new in let ⟨k, k′⟩ = new in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close w′) in              -- waits forever
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force sink) k′) in
       (force refresh) ⟨w, k⟩
examples.meaning: Each round links the partner of the waiting end to a new channel. The waiting thread then faces a new end with a full counter, and no counter decreases to $0$. Each link uses one ticket of its thread and no step creates tickets, so the program has no lock-free typing.

deviations.reason: To be mechanized.

examples.title: A waiting chain that grows forever
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which a chain of waiting threads grows forever.
examples.code:
grow = !(f = λw. let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in                 -- c below the point of w
                 let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in let ∗ = spawn (λ_. recvclose d′) in
                 let ∗ = close (send ⟨∗, d⟩) in              -- one session action
                 let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force f) c′) in
                 let ∗ = close c in close w)                 -- waits on its child
main = let ⟨w, w′⟩ = new in let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close w′) in (force grow) w
-- every thread waits on the one it spawned, close w′ never proceeds
examples.meaning: Each thread spawns a child, waits on it, and the child does the same. Each wait is at a point below the point of the previous one, and the chain grows forever. A well-founded world has no infinite descending chain, and lock-free soundness assumes a well-founded world.

deviations.reason: To be mechanized.
